Adopts 'Super Intelligence' term for new processors, retrofits it for old ones too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tesla has disclosed its revamped AI accelerator roadmap that sheds some light on the future of the company's chip development efforts. The Elon Musk company expects that its 6th Generation inference accelerator will bring 80X more compute performance than the existing 4th Generation chip, whereas its D3 training accelerator will cease to use SRAM-centric architecture in favor of a multi-chiplet design with stacked HBM. Also, Tesla has adopted the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence for its AI accelerators, renaming them with SI monikers. Musk recently confirmed SpaceXAI would be redubbed SpaceXSI for the same reason.

Wait a minute… I thought @elonmusk ’s Tesla chips were called AI4, AI5, and AI6. But in this latest presentation, they’re now labeled SI4, SI5, and SI6. Then I remembered: President Trump wants to replace “Artificial Intelligence” (AI) with “Super Intelligence” (SI). Looks like Elon Musk may already be embracing the new terminology. 🤔November 4, 2026

Perhaps the most interesting development in Tesla's AI hardware roadmap is the re-emergence of the in-house developed Dojo training accelerator after Elon Musk cancelled the whole wafer-level Dojo project in August, 2025, and then said SpaceX and xAI would exclusively use Nvidia hardware in August, 2026, both in its terrestrial and extraterrestrial data centers. Yet, the 3rd Generation Dojo will be considerably different from the first two generations, Dojo D1 and Dojo D2.

Tesla describes its next-generation Dojo 3 (D3) training accelerator as a chiplet-based design that combines 2.5D and 3D packaging technologies with stacked HBM. This represents a substantial departure from the original Dojo D1 system-on-wafer architecture, which relied on distributed on-chip SRAM and interconnected 25 D1 processors with 11 GB of SRAM using wafer-scale packaging technology. The adoption of HBM suggests that Tesla intends to substantially increase memory capacity, as modern AI models consume extreme amounts of memory to store parameters, activations, and intermediate data, making SRAM unattractive from a capacity standpoint. The use of HBM simplifies memory scaling but introduces different latency, bandwidth, packaging, and power trade-offs. Yet, it remains unclear whether the company has abandoned wafer-scale integration altogether.

On the one hand, it is possible to stack custom HBM modules on top of logic dies interconnected using wafer-scale packaging technology. On the other hand, wafer-level integration is expensive and makes the most sense for select use cases, which include SRAM-centric architectures. Stacking HBM atop wafer-scale interconnected logic dies adds further design complexities, cooling challenges, manufacturing complexity (i.e., potentially reducing yields), long-term reliability concerns, and ultimately costs. While most of the challenges can be resolved by adding redundancy and refining process technologies, this all comes at a cost, making wafer-scaling less likely for D3.

Tesla has yet to disclose D3's compute performance, memory capacity, manufacturing process, or development schedule. At the same time, it claims that its Dojo D3 will be optimized for 'space, training, and scaling,' which means the unit will offer decent performance and will be easy to scale (which again points to a more conventional architecture of accelerators rather than to wafer-scale packaging). More intriguingly, the D3 is also set to be optimized for extraterrestrial deployments, which probably means radiation hardening for at least select SKUs.

Another interesting detail in the roadmap is the disclosure of approximate compute performance of Tesla's 6th Generation inference accelerator (SI6): 80X compute improvement over HW4 and 9X more memory over HW4. Depending on how HW4 performance is measured (read on for explanation), we are talking about 17,280 – 46,080 TOPS (trillion operations per second), or 17.28 – 46.08 POPS (quadrillion operations per second), though we do not know anything about data formats supported by SI6. Of course, these are estimates, so take them with a grain of salt. To put the numbers into context, Nvidia's Rubin GPU offers 50 NVFP4 PFLOPS for inference, 35 NVFP4 PFLOPS for training, and 17.5 FP8/FP6 PFLOPS. Meanwhile, Rubin is shipping to customers today, whereas SI6 is due in 2029 – 2030. There are some additional details about SI6, which we will discuss below.

Tesla's existing 4th Generation inference processor used in the company's automobiles today (which was originally called HW4, then renamed to AI4, then to SI4) is made by Samsung Foundry using its 7nm-class process technology and relies on conventional flip-chip ball grid array (FCBGA) packaging (note that the alleged Tesla slide contains a mistake and claims that the unit is made using a 5nm-class node) as well as presumably 16 GB of GDDR6 memory. The company describes the processor as the current benchmark for its Full Self-Driving (FSD) technology, which makes it the baseline against which performance of future generations is measured. Meanwhile, Tesla does not officially disclose the chip's absolute compute performance numbers, memory capacity, or power consumption, which makes comparison hard. Elon Musk once said that HW4 is 3X – 8X more powerful than HW3, which was officially rated at 72 TOPS, making HW4 a 216 – 576 TOPS ASIC (note that these are estimates).

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

As expected, the slide re-confirms that the upcoming 5th Generation inference accelerator called SI5 (aka HW5 aka AI5) will be manufactured using 3nm- and 2nm-class process technologies at TSMC and Samsung Foundry, respectively, and will adopt a multi-chip module (MCM) design, marking a departure from the conventional packaging approach used for HW4. Tesla expects SI5 to deliver a 40X performance improvement over HW4, which will be a result of an eightfold increase in compute capabilities (driven by considerably denser process technologies and more execution units) and a fivefold gain from silicon optimization, according to Elon Musk, which points to 8,640 – 23,040 TOPS (an estimated figure), depending on how one counts performance of HW4. Meanwhile, the processor is expected to consume from 250W to 800W depending on application, so making performance estimates at this point is not exactly a good business. Meanwhile, the processor will also feature six times more memory than its predecessor (i.e., 96 GB). Depending on the memory type used (GDDR6 or GDDR7), the Tesla SI5 can offer memory bandwidth between 768 GB/s and 1.536 GB/s.

Moving on to the Tesla's 6th Generation inference accelerator (SI6), which is set to further increase compute performance to 80 times that of HW4 and feature eight times more memory than the current-generation processor. This could translate to 17.28 – 46.08 POPS (quadrillion operations per second), depending on how to count HW4 performance, and 144 GB of memory, which is significant performance and amount of memory for an AI accelerator.

Tesla has already inked a deal with Samsung Foundry to make its 6th Generation inference accelerators through 2033, and the new slide reveals that the unit will be made using a 2nm-class process technology. Given the fact that the chip is due in 2029 – 2030 and Samsung's recently updated foundry roadmap, we are probably talking about automotive-grade SF2A, performance-enhanced SF2P, or even SF2Z with backside power delivery. Meanwhile, a thing that strikes the eye with the SI6 is that Tesla does not envision the chip to be produced at Terafab using Intel's 14A fabrication process in the 2030s.

SI6 will retain the multi-chip module (MCM) approach introduced with AI5/SI5/HW5, which seems rational as it will be able to leverage experience it is going to get with its 5th Generation inference accelerator and retain relatively reasonable packaging costs. Many automakers are considering adoption of multi-chiplet designs and HBM memory for their next-generation system-in-packages (SiPs), which will drive their costs. It remains to be seen when Tesla adopts HBM for its inference accelerators, but probably not with SI6.

#10370. Falcon Perception

TL;DR — Falcon Perception is a 0.6B-parameter early-fusion Transformer for open-vocabulary grounding and segmentation from natural language prompts. The model processes image patches + text in one sequence using a hybrid attention mask, and produces variable numbers of instances with a small, structured token interface and lightweight output heads. On SA-Co, Falcon Perception reaches 68.0 Macro-F1 (vs. 62.3 for SAM 3) with the main remaining gap being presence calibration (MCC 0.64 vs. 0.82). We also introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that breaks down performance by capability (attributes, OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relations) and by dense long-context crowded scenes.

We also relase Falcon OCR, a 0.3B-parameter model which reaches a score of 80.3 and 88.6 on the olmOCR benchmark and OmniDocBench respectively, while having the highest throughput of any open source OCR model.

This post is a brief, practical write-up of what we built, why we built it this way, and what we learned along the way.

Many open-vocabulary perception systems are built as modular pipelines: a (often frozen) vision backbone extracts features, a separate fusion/decoder stage combines them with language, and additional components handle matching and post-processing. This family of designs works well in many settings, but it comes with trade-offs: it can be hard to scale cleanly, hard to attribute improvements to the right component, and easy to accumulate complexity as we add a new fix for each failure mode.

We asked a simpler question: can a single early-fusion Transformer backbone handle both perception and language modeling, if we choose the right attention pattern, output interface, and training signal?

In our experiments, the answer is largely yes. The rest of this post describes the main design choices and the evidence behind them.

A single autoregressive Transformer processes a unified sequence of image patches, text, and task tokens. The model predicts object properties in a fixed order: → → . Bounding box coordinates and sizes are decoded via specialized heads and re-injected as Fourier features. High-resolution segmentation masks are generated by a dot product between the token and upsampled image features.

At its core, Falcon Perception is a dense Transformer that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space from the first layer. Instead of a separate vision backbone followed by a late-fusion decoder, we keep a single backbone and rely on masking and a lightweight output interface to make the dense prediction problem tractable.

Images and text have different structure: pixels are 2D and benefit from bidirectional context, while the prediction interface is naturally sequential. We address this with a hybrid attention mask:

This allows the same backbone to behave like a bidirectional visual encoder on image tokens, while still supporting autoregressive prediction over task tokens.

Dense perception is not a fixed-size prediction problem: an image may contain zero instances or hundreds. Autoregressive generation gives a clean variable-length interface, but fully autoregressive dense generation (e.g., polygons or high-resolution masks token-by-token) quickly becomes expensive.

We use a small structured interface, Chain-of-Perception, which decomposes each instance into three steps:

This ordering is deliberate. Committing to geometry first reduces ambiguity (“which instance?”), and makes the mask prediction step closer to pixel refinement conditioned on the resolved object.

The backbone is shared, while decoding uses lightweight heads tailored to the output type:

Coordinate & Size Heads use Fourier feature encoding : mapping continuous coordinates through a random Gaussian projection into a high-dimensional sinusoidal space. This overcomes the spectral bias of neural networks, yielding more precise localization than discrete binning alone. Decoded coordinates are re-injected into the sequence as conditioning for subsequent tokens.

Segmentation Head computes a dot product between the token’s hidden state and content-aware upsampled image features. Because the token is produced after geometry and has access to early-fused visual context, we can avoid the separate mask-query machinery and Hungarian matching that often appears in decoder-based instance segmentation training.

Existing referring-expression benchmarks like RefCOCO are saturated — models routinely hit 90%+ — and they conflate what went wrong. Did the model fail because it can't read text? Can't understand spatial relationships? Can't handle a crowd?

We introduce PBench, a diagnostic benchmark that separates samples by the dominant capability required:

Each sample targets one dominant capability: OCR prompts avoid spatial qualifiers, and spatial prompts avoid in-image text disambiguators. This yields a capability profile rather than a single opaque score, and makes it easier to decide where to invest next (data, training curriculum, or post-training).

Rather than training from random weights (which in our ablations was unstable for segmentation), Falcon Perception initializes via multi-teacher distillation. Two strong vision teachers contribute complementary signals:

The distilled initialization achieves 74.25% zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet-1k and 85.11% linear-probe mIoU on Pascal VOC, providing a strong visual foundation before perception-specific training.

We build the training set through a multi-stage pipeline:

We maintain a strict 1:1 ratio of positive to negative samples. This makes presence calibration a first-class target: the model should reliably say “absent,” not only draw masks when confident.

Stage 1 — In-Context Listing (450 GT): The model learns to autoregressively list scene inventories — predicting text expressions and their locations. Full causal attention between queries enables learning of object co-occurrence ("fork, then knife, then plate"). This builds broad scene understanding.

Stage 2 — Task Alignment (225 GT): The attention mask is modified so queries can no longer see each other, simulating independent queries at inference time. Loss on text tokens is masked, focusing gradient signal entirely on presence classification and localization. This stage transitions from "scene understanding" to "answer this specific question."

Stage 3 — Long-Context Finetuning (10 GT): A short phase with the mask limit raised to 600 per expression and a minimal constant learning rate. This adapts the model for extreme crowd density without forgetting earlier capabilities.

Key design choices validated through ablations:

On the SA-Co open-vocabulary segmentation benchmark, Falcon Perception (0.6B parameters) achieves 68.0 Macro-F1, compared to 62.3 for SAM 3, with large gains on attribute-heavy (+8.2), food & drink (+12.2), and sports equipment (+4.0) splits. At the same time, Falcon Perception lags SAM 3 on presence calibration (MCC: 0.64 vs 0.82), which is the clearest remaining improvement axis.

Here's an example output — the prompt "Falcon" produces precise instance masks:

Falcon Perception also performs well for reffering expressions, able to correctly segment the burger with a black bun in each frame of the video:

This is where the early-fusion design shows the largest differences:

On simple objects, the gap is modest. As prompts become more compositional—requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, or relational binding—the gap widens.

In our PBench Dense split, Falcon Perception (0.6B) substantially outperforms generalist VLM baselines (e.g., 72.6 vs 8.9 for Qwen3-VL-30B in our evaluation setup), and matches or exceeds the 8B model on spatial and relational tiers.

As prompts grow more compositional — requiring OCR-guided disambiguation, spatial constraints, relational binding, or scaling to hundreds of instances — the early-fusion advantage becomes visually clear:

"168 wine bottles": Falcon Perception identifies the bottles labeled "168", while SAM 3 highlights every bottle. "Honolulu direction sign": Falcon reads the text to find the right sign.

"Lower meat skewer on left grill," "black car to the right of red car at bottom," "Belgian flag on the left" — Falcon Perception resolves the correct instance from spatial constraints. SAM 3 predicts false positives for multiple candidates.

"Pastry next to brown round bread," "person using phone," "person holding helmet in hand" — Falcon Perception identifies the interacting instance. SAM 3 highlights all instances of the object class, ignoring the relational constraint.

"Snow goose," "pigeon," "colorful canned drinks" — Falcon Perception autoregressively segments hundreds of instances. SAM 3's fixed-size decoder runs out of query tokens beyond ~200 instances.

Modern OCR has moved well beyond extracting text from clean scans. Today's systems must handle multi-column layouts, mathematical formulas, tables, charts, and multilingual content — all in one pass. Most competitive OCR VLMs tackle this with a familiar recipe: a vision encoder feeding a separate text decoder, plus task-specific glue. These systems work, but they tend to be large (1B–3B+ parameters).

We took a different path: reuse the same early-fusion dense Transformer from Falcon Perception, but train a smaller 0.3B-parameter variant from scratch specifically for OCR. The result is Falcon OCR — a single backbone that processes image patches and text tokens in a shared parameter space with the same hybrid attention mask (bidirectional for image tokens, causal for text tokens), and switches tasks through prompts rather than additional modules.

We trained from scratch (no multi-teacher distillation) because the visual features OCR needs — fine-grained glyph recognition, stroke-level discrimination — differ substantially from the object-level features useful for segmentation. Starting fresh lets the backbone develop text-optimized representations from the ground up.

We train on a curated English-language mixture spanning three core tasks: general document text parsing (digital PDFs, old scans, typewritten documents), mathematical and scientific formula recognition, and table structure recognition. The mixture also includes handwriting, real-world scene text, and synthetic samples generated from rendered LaTeX and HTML sources. The training objective is pure next-token prediction on structured text outputs.

Training proceeds in two phases: a long pre-training phase at constant learning rate where the model learns core OCR capabilities across all element types, followed by a short cosine-decay finetuning phase where the learning rate is annealed to near zero.

We evaluate on olmOCR (binary correctness checks across diverse inputs) and OmniDocBench (continuous metrics over full-page parses). All comparison models are significantly larger and/or use proprietary infrastructure. At 80.3% on olmOCR with only 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is within 1.7 points of the top system and leads all models on Multi-Column (87.1%) and Tables (90.3%). On OmniDocBench it scores 88.64 overall, ahead of DeepSeek OCR v2, GPT 5.2, and Mistral OCR 3.

At 0.3B parameters, Falcon OCR is roughly 3x smaller than 0.9B-class OCR VLMs, which translates directly into higher serving throughput. Measured on a single A100-80GB with vLLM at high concurrency:

The compact footprint and vLLM integration (continuous batching, PagedAttention, optimized CUDA kernels) make it practical for large-scale document digitization where millions of pages need processing.

More broadly, these results suggest that the early-fusion single-stack Transformer is a viable alternative to the "vision encoder plus text decoder" recipe for OCR. One backbone, shared parameter space, one decoding interface, and better data and training signals rather than increasingly complex pipelines. We hope this encourages more work in this direction.

Falcon OCR processes images captured under challenging real-world conditions with varying lighting, diverse text semantics (mathematical formulae, structured tables, handwritten notes), and complex document layouts, to produce structured text output.

Falcon OCR extracts text from handwritten documents and real-world photographs with variable lighting, orientation, and content complexity.

Falcon OCR accurately reproduces cell entries and structural layout from tables of varying formats and complexity.

Falcon OCR correctly transcribes mathematical expressions ranging from simple equations to multi-line derivations with nested operators.

Falcon OCR preserves reading order and structural fidelity when extracting text from documents with multi-column layouts, figures, and footnotes.

The release includes an inference stack built on PyTorch’s FlexAttention, which makes it practical to express the custom attention patterns and efficiently serve packed variable-length sequences.

In our setup on an H100, typical latencies are on the order of ~100ms prefill, ~200ms upsampling (0ms if cached), and ~50ms decode for a handful of instances. (These numbers depend on resolution, sequence length, and the number of predicted instances.)

For the Falcon-OCR model, we also provide a vLLM docker server for fast deployment and MLX integration for Apple-Silicon

Please check out the github repo for details.

Falcon Perception is intentionally minimal: one backbone, one objective family, and small heads only where outputs are continuous and dense. The working assumption is that most gains should come from data, compute, and training signals, rather than continually expanding the pipeline with specialized modules.

The architecture doesn't block any obvious scaling path: add more images and harder prompts for better grounding, mix in text-only data for better language, increase context length for denser scenes. It's still just one sequence model.

Falcon Perception is developed by the Falcon Vision Team at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII), Abu Dhabi, UAE.

If you use Falcon-Perception, please cite

#10369. Phone by Google 246 beta brings gradient icon redesign on Android

Following the Messages update earlier this week, Phone by Google has received its redesigned gradient icon in the beta channel.

Version 246 of Phone by Google — as the app is still officially called to presumably avoid the Pixel overlap that comes with “Google Phone” — is rolling out today to the beta channel.

Compared to the previous iteration, the handset in the new icon is a bit larger. Otherwise, the general shape remains the same and shouldn’t cause any confusion.

By leveraging gradients for the earpiece and mouthpiece, the new design feels flatter and lighter than the old one. Additionally, the darker blue shade has been removed entirely. Google says the “app icon is now crisper, clearer, and designed to look sharp on your home screen.”

We also refreshed the coloring, spacing, and gradients to bring the icon closer in line with the modern look of the rest of the Google ecosystem. Now, the Phone app blends seamlessly with all your other Google tools, making your screen feel cohesive and clean.

There are no other changes to the app with this update. Zooming out, Google has yet to roll out the restored Contacts tab to stable users as of today.

Phone by Google 246 should see a stable rollout in the coming weeks. You can join the beta via the Play Store listing.

#10368. How to Build a Typed AI Pipeline With Jev and Clairic.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A support email lands: "Order NW-47790, the tent poles snapped on the first night, I paid $389 and I want every cent back today or I'm disputing the charge."

To act on that, your code needs answers to a handful of small questions. Is it a refund request? How urgent is it? Should a person handle it? What's the order number? How much money is involved? It's the same problem whether you're sorting a support inbox or building a custom chatbot that has to work out what each customer is asking for.

The usual move is to send the whole email to a chat model with a prompt that ends "respond in JSON", then validate whatever comes back. It works, but you're paying a model built to write essays to fill in five fields, and you're parsing its guess at a schema.

System One models are built for exactly this kind of job. In this tutorial we'll build a small support inbox pipeline with two of them: Jev from TypeSafe makes the decisions, and Clairic from Cloudflare reads the values. Plain TypeScript then turns their answers into an action. No prompt engineering for output formats, and no JSON repair.

The name comes from Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow. System 1 is the fast, intuitive kind of thinking you use to read a face or a sign. System 2 is the slow, deliberate kind you use for long division.

A System One model is an AI model that understands natural language but doesn't generate text. You give it some input (the state) and a set of typed questions, and it gives back typed answers with probabilities. There's no free text to parse, because the model can only answer in the shape you asked for.

That's different from asking a chat model for structured output. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema shows how to constrain a chat model and validate its JSON with Zod. With a System One model, the type is the interface: a yes/no question comes back as a probability, a pick-one question comes back as one of your options, and a date comes back as a date.

Jev and Clairic are both System One models, but they do different jobs, and that's what makes them a good pair.

Jev can't hand you an order number, and Clairic has no way to pick from a list of options or answer yes or no. Give each one the job it's built for.

If you've read SitePoint's Jev and LangChain tutorial, you've seen Jev deciding which model handles an agent's request. Here we'll use it on the incoming text itself.

Five made-up emails for a made-up outdoor gear store go in. For each one:

Both models read the same email, so they run at the same time.

Put the three values in your environment:

No SDKs are needed. Both models are a single fetch call.

Here's the test inbox. Each email is there to test a different path through the rules:

Jev takes a state (the email) and a set of named questions. We'll ask three, one of each type:

All three questions go in one request. Jev reads the email once and answers every question in parallel, so adding a question costs very little:

We pin jev-1.14.0 rather than the jev-latest alias. Your thresholds get tuned against one version's probabilities, so you want to choose when that version changes.

For the angry tent email, Jev came back with:

(Trimmed: the real response also includes the probability of every option and level.)

Clairic takes the same state, plus a set of typed fields instead of questions:

reference_date anchors relative dates like "the 14th" or "last Monday". In production, pass the date the email arrived.

Each answer comes back with three things worth using:

For the "where is it?" email, Clairic read the deadline like this:

"The 14th" became a full date, worked out from the reference date. Text fields like order_number also come back as character spans of the original email. The value is copied from the input, not generated, so it can't invent an order number that isn't there.

The two models don't depend on each other, so send both requests together:

The time for each email is whichever model is slower, not the two added together.

This is the part a chat model usually ends up doing badly: the business rules. Here they're ordinary code you can read, test, and change without touching a prompt:

Notice that the model's confidence sits right next to the business rule. A $18.95 refund is only automatic if Clairic is sure about both the order number and the amount. Raising the refund limit or the confidence bar is a one-line change, and you don't need to call either model again to see what it would do. Save the answers and replay them.

Every email went where it should. The whole run used 2,703 input tokens on Jev and 2,292 on Clairic, about US$0.0003 in total. At that rate, 10,000 support emails would cost roughly US$0.70.

The interesting part of the run wasn't the right answers. It was the two wrong ones.

"From last Monday." The run used 2 November 2026 as the reference date, which is a Monday. "Last Monday" means 26 October, but Clairic answered 2026-11-02, the reference date itself. Its confidence on that answer was 0.54, compared with 0.99 or higher on almost every other value in the run.

"A couple of weeks ago." Clairic turned this into 2026-10-19, which is a fair reading but still a guess. Its confidence was 0.43.

Neither date changed any action, because the rules only trust values at 0.9 or above. That's the habit to build: a value under your bar counts as unknown. A chat model returning JSON would have handed you "2026-11-02" with the same certainty as everything else.

One more catch: Clairic copied the order number as #NW-48213, hash included, because that's how the customer wrote it. Text values are spans of the input, so normalising them is your code's job. That's one line of code.

System One models handle the reading and the routing. They don't hold a conversation. Once an email is routed, something still has to write the reply, ask a follow-up question, or explain a returns policy in the customer's own words. That's where a chat model earns its cost.

The split that works is: System One models decide, code applies the rules, and a chat model only gets the cases where words matter.

We built a support inbox triage pipeline from two small models and some ordinary code:

Each email took about half a second and cost less than a hundredth of a cent. Most importantly, the two answers that would have been wrong came back flagged as unsure.

The full code is about 160 lines with no dependencies. Try adding a fourth Jev question (does the customer mention a photo?) or an estimate field in Clairic (how many days until the trip?), and see how little the rest of the pipeline has to change.

#10366. Welcome Gemma 4: Frontier multimodal intelligence on device

The Gemma 4 family of multimodal models by Google DeepMind is out on Hugging Face, with support for your favorite agents, inference engines, and fine-tuning libraries 🤗

These models are the real deal: truly open with Apache 2 licenses, high quality with pareto frontier arena scores, multimodal including audio, and sizes you can use everywhere including on-device. Gemma 4 builds on advances from previous families and makes them click together. In our tests with pre-release checkpoints we have been impressed by their capabilities, to the extent that we struggled to find good fine-tuning examples because they are so good out of the box.

We collaborated with Google and the community to make them available everywhere: transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, WebGPU, Rust; you name it. This blog post will show you how to build with your favorite tools so let us know what you think!

Similar to Gemma-3n, Gemma 4 supports image, text, and audio inputs, and generates text responses. The text decoder is based on the Gemma model with support for long context windows. The image encoder is similar to the one from Gemma 3 but with two crucial improvements: variable aspect ratios, and configurable number of image token inputs to find your sweet spot between speed, memory, and quality. All models support images (or video) and text inputs, while the small variants (E2B, E4B) and the 12B Unified model support audio as well.

Gemma 4 comes in five sizes, all base and instruction fine-tuned:

Gemma 4 leverages several architecture components used in previous Gemma versions and other open models, and leaves out complex or inconclusive features such as Altup. The combination is a mix designed to be highly compatible across libraries and devices, that can efficiently support long context and agentic use cases, whilst being ideal for quantization.

As shown in the benchmarks above, this feature mix (combined with the training data and recipe) enables the 31B dense model to achieve an estimated LMArena score (text only) of 1452, while the 26B MoE reaches 1441 with just 4B active parameters 🤯. As we'll see, multimodal operation is comparatively as good as text generation, at least in informal and subjective tests.

These are the main architecture characteristics in Gemma 4:

One of the most distinctive features in smaller Gemma 4 models is Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which was introduced previously in Gemma-3n. In a standard transformer, each token gets a single embedding vector at input, and the same initial representation is what the residual stream builds on across all layers, forcing the embedding to frontload everything the model might need. PLE adds a parallel, lower-dimensional conditioning pathway alongside the main residual stream. For each token, it produces a small dedicated vector for every layer by combining two signals: a token-identity component (from an embedding lookup) and a context-aware component (from a learned projection of the main embeddings). Each decoder layer then uses its corresponding vector to modulate the hidden states via a lightweight residual block after attention and feed-forward. This gives each layer its own channel to receive token-specific information only when it becomes relevant, rather than requiring everything to be packed into a single upfront embedding. Because the PLE dimension is much smaller than the main hidden size, this adds meaningful per-layer specialization at modest parameter cost. For multimodal inputs (images, audio, video), PLE is computed before soft tokens are merged into the embedding sequence — since PLE relies on token IDs that are lost once multimodal features replace the placeholders. Multimodal positions use the pad token ID, effectively receiving neutral per-layer signals.

The shared KV cache is an efficiency optimization that reduces both compute and memory during inference. The last num_kv_shared_layers layers of the model don't compute their own key and value projections. Instead, they reuse the K and V tensors from the last non-shared layer of the same attention type (sliding or full).

In practice, this has a minimal impact on quality while being much more efficient (in terms of both memory and compute) for long context generation and on-device use.

The Gemma 4 12B Unified model has no separate vision or audio encoder. Instead, raw image patches and audio waveforms are projected directly into the LLM's embedding space through lightweight linear layers, and all modalities flow into a single decoder-only transformer. This reduces multimodal latency and allows the whole model to be fine-tuned in one pass. The checkpoint size makes it deployment-friendly on consumer hardware.

We saw in our tests that Gemma 4 supports comprehensive multimodal capabilities out of the box. We don't know what was the training mix, but we had success using it for tasks such as OCR, speech-to-text, object detection, or pointing. It also supports text-only and multimodal function calling, reasoning, code completion and correction.

Here, we show a few inference examples across different model sizes. You can run them conveniently with this notebook. We encourage you to try the demos and share them below this blog!

Gemma 4 was trained with a specific convention to interleave input modalities:

To be specific, this is a correct fragment that prepares inputs for the chat template:

The audio inference snippets in this post don't follow this convention, as they were written before this guidance was confirmed. We are keeping them as originally written so result tables remain reproducible. For your own code, prefer the order above.

We test Gemma 4 on GUI element detection and pointing across different sizes, with the following image and text prompt: "What's the bounding box for the "view recipe" element in the image?"

With this prompt, the model natively responds in JSON format with the detected bounding boxes - no need for specific instructions or grammar-constrained generation. We found the coordinates refer to an image size of 1000x1000, relative to the input dimensions.

We visualize the outputs below for your convenience. We parse the bounding boxes from the returned JSON: json\n[\n {"box_2d": [171, 75, 245, 308], "label": "view recipe element"}\n]\n

We test models to detect everyday objects, here we ask them to detect the bike and compare different model outputs. As in the previous case, we parse the bounding box from the json and translate to image space coordinates.

We asked Gemma 4 to write HTML code to reconstruct a page we made with Gemini 3. Below you can find the code to do this, we enable thinking and ask each model to generate up to 4000 new tokens, to make it foolproof.

Smaller Gemma 4 models can take in videos with audio while larger ones can take in videos without audio. While the models are not explicitly post-trained on videos, they can understand videos both with and without audio. The model is particularly strong in audios

We have tested all models on captioning. All checkpoints perform very well and accurately capture nuance in complex scenerios. Here's the image we use, with the prompt "Write single detailed caption for this image.".

These models are trained to answer questions about speech in audio. Music and non-speech sounds were not part of the training data.

Here is an example if you want to do transcription:

Gemma 4 comes with day-0 support for many open-source inference engines, and is ideal for tool calling and agents! We also release ONNX checkpoints that can run on many hardware backends, allowing use cases on edge devices or in browser!

Gemma 4 comes with first-class transformers support from the get-go 🤗. This integration allows using the model with other libraries like bitsandbytes, PEFT and TRL. Make sure to install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to infer with the small Gemma 4 models is through the any-to-any pipeline. You can initialize it as follows.

You can then pass in images and text as follows.

When inferring with videos, you can include the audio track using the load_audio_from_video argument.

Going a level lower, you can load Gemma 4 using the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class, especially useful for fine-tuning. The built-in chat template takes care of formatting the inputs correctly, please make sure you use it to prevent subtle mistakes when building the prompt manually.

Gemma 4 models come with image+text support in llama.cpp from the get-go! This unlocks using Gemma 4 with all of your favorite local apps: llama-cpp server, lmstudio, Jan as well as coding agents like Pi across many backends such as Metal and CUDA.

You can then start a server compatible with the OpenAI API Replace the quantization scheme at the end of the command with the precision of your choice.

Check out this link for more options on combining llama.cpp with different coding agents and local apps. Find all the GGUF checkpoints in this collection.

We worked on making sure the new models work locally with agents like openclaw, hermes, pi, and open code. All thanks to llama.cpp! Run the following to try Gemma 4 right away.

For open code define a ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:

transformers.js enables running Gemma 4 right inside browser. You can check out the model card to see text-only, image & text, audio & text inference in detail here. We also shipped a demo for you to test the model here.

Full multimodal support of Gemma 4 is available using the open-source mlx-vlm library. Here's how to ask the model to describe an image:

mlx-vlm supports TurboQuant, which delivers the same accuracy as the uncompressed baseline while using ~4x less active memory and running a lot faster end-to-end. This makes long-context inference practical on Apple Silicon without sacrificing quality. Use it like this:

For audio examples and more details, please check the MLX collection.

mistral.rs is a Rust-native inference engine with day-0 Gemma 4 support across all modalities (text, image, video, audio) and builtin tool-calling and agentic functionality. Install mistral.rs:

You can then start an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server:

Find all models here. Please, follow the instructions in the model cards for installation and inference guidelines.

Google has released Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) drafters for the Gemma 4 family: small assistant models that accelerate inference via speculative decoding. The drafter proposes several future tokens at once, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass. You get the same outputs as the target model, just faster — no quality loss, no changes to reasoning behaviour. Reported end-to-end speedups go up to ~3x depending on hardware, batch size, and workload.

Assistants are available for all four Gemma 4 sizes (E2B, E4B, 26B A4B, 31B). They share the KV cache with the target model to avoid recomputing context, and the smaller edge variants additionally use an embedder clustering trick to keep memory and compute low on-device.

Find the checkpoints in the Gemma 4 collection and the mlx-community collection.

Alongside the autoregressive Gemma 4 family, Google DeepMind is releasing DiffusionGemma, a multimodal model that generates text using discrete diffusion instead of token-by-token autoregression. It's built on the same 26B A4B Mixture-of-Experts foundation (25.2B total / 3.8B active parameters, 8 active experts out of 128 plus 1 shared), takes text and image inputs, generates text, and supports up to 256K context — all under the same Apache 2.0 license.

Where a standard causal LM emits one token at a time, DiffusionGemma denoises whole blocks of tokens in parallel. The architecture is encoder-decoder: an autoregressive encoder prefills the prompt and builds the KV cache, while a decoder applies bidirectional attention over a "canvas" of 256 tokens. During multi-canvas sampling, the model iteratively denoises a full canvas with a diffusion sampler; once a canvas is finalized it's encoded and appended to the KV cache, then the next canvas begins. This block-autoregressive approach increases generation speed.

The headline benefit is throughput: parallel denoising generates roughly 15–20 tokens per forward pass, reaching per-user generation speeds exceeding 1100 tokens/second at low batch sizes (H100, FP8). Inference compute is adaptive too — simpler prompts and structured tasks like code need fewer denoising steps, so tokens-per-second scales with task complexity. It keeps the broader Gemma 4 toolkit: thinking mode, function calling, long context, native system prompts, and image understanding (OCR, document parsing, object detection, pointing) at variable aspect ratios and resolutions.

Benchmarks show an expected trade-off between speed and evaluation metrics — DiffusionGemma trails the autoregressive 26B A4B on most tasks (e.g. MMLU Pro 77.6% vs 82.6%, AIME 2026 69.1% vs 88.3%, GPQA Diamond 73.2% vs 82.3%) in exchange for its large speed advantage, while edging ahead on a few (HLE no tools 11.0% vs 8.7%).

Getting started looks just like the rest of Gemma 4, via the dedicated diffusion class:

For best results, Google recommends the Entropy-Bounded (EB) sampler with adaptive stopping (up to 48 denoising steps, a temperature schedule decaying from 0.8 → 0.4, and an entropy bound of 0.1 for token selection). As with Gemma 4, place image content before text in your prompt, and toggle reasoning with the <|think|> control token.

Gemma 4 models are ideal for fine-tuning in your favorite tools and platforms and at any budget.

Gemma 4 is fully supported for fine-tuning with TRL. To celebrate, TRL has been upgraded with support for multimodal tool responses when interacting with environments, meaning models can now receive images back from tools during training, not just text.

To showcase this, we've built an example training script where Gemma 4 learns to drive in the CARLA simulator. The model sees the road through a camera, decides what to do and learns from the outcome. After training, it consistently changes lanes to avoid pedestrians. The same approach works for any task where a model needs to see and act: robotics, web browsing, or other interactive environments.

Additionally, we have prepared an example on how to fine-tune Gemma 4 with TRL on Vertex AI using SFT, to showcase how to extend the function calling capabilities, whilst freezing both the vision and audio towers. The examples include how to build a custom Docker container with latest Transformers, TRL, etc. with CUDA support on Google Cloud, and how to run it via Vertex AI Serverless Training Jobs.

You can find the complete example in the "Hugging Face on Google Cloud" docs at https://hf.co/docs/google-cloud/examples/vertex-ai-notebooks-fine-tune-gemma-4.

If you want to fine tune and run a Gemma 4 model in a UI, try out Unsloth Studio. It runs locally or on Google Colab. First, install and start the app:

Then select any of the Gemma 4 models from the hub.

We have shipped demos for you to try different Gemma 4 models. We include demos based on the transformers implementation for E4B, 12B Unified, 26B/A4B MoE, and 31B dense models. There's also a WebGPU demo with transformers.js 🚀

Gemma 4 models demonstrate exceptional performance across diverse benchmarks, from reasoning and coding to vision and long-context tasks. The graph below shows model performance vs size, with Gemma 4 models forming an impressive Pareto frontier:

Here are detailed benchmark results for the instruction-tuned models:

This work wouldn't have been possible without Google's extensive contribution with the model artefact, but also the significant effort contributing the model to transformers in an effort to standardize it. The open-source ecosystem is now more complete, with a very capable, freely-licensed, open-source model. The Gemma 4 transformers integration was handled by Cyril, Raushan, Eustache, Arthur, Lysandre. one gap worth flagging for anyone building on Gemma 4's function calling for real-world deployments: when the model generates a function call, there's currently no verifiable record that a human principal authorized that specific action. a compromised system prompt or injected instruction produces a call that's indistinguishable from legitimate delegation at the tool interface.

i opened a PR on the gemma-cookbook repo today that adds a drop-in HDP middleware layer to address this, sits between Gemma 4's function call output and tool execution, verifies Ed25519-signed delegation tokens, classifies actions by irreversibility (Class 0–3), and blocks unauthorized calls pre-execution.

for edge/robotics deployments (E2B on Jetson Nano / Raspberry Pi directing actuators), there's a companion HDP-P extension covering the physical layer.

#10365. Samsung brings back free doubled storage discount on Galaxy Z Fold 8

Samsung is running its much-loved “double the storage” promo on its Galaxy Z Fold 8 right now.

A common pre-order perk over the years on Samsung Galaxy devices has been doubled storage at no added cost. Basically, get the next tier up at the cost of the base model. Samsung has brought this back occasionally after pre-orders end, but usually with a catch or two.

That’s what we’re seeing right now on the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

You can currently get the Galaxy Z Fold 8 with “double the storage on select colors” from Samsung.com right now. That limited color is “Lavender,” but the other catch is that it also only applies to the upper 1TB model.

Getting that for $400 off is nothing to shake a stick at – it’s a very good deal. It’s just that most Fold 8 buyers are probably already going to balk at the $1,899 price of the base model, especially when Amazon still has it for $1,599 (or $1,799 for the 512GB model). Amazon doesn’t sell the Fold 8 with 1TB of storage at all.

This isn’t the only device that’s offering doubled storage, though, as Samsung.com is also offering the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra in “Green Shadow” with the same limited-time offer. This time it’s the 512GB model for the price of the 256GB model, $2,099.

Both offers are still eligible for trade-in discounts of up to $800 or, if you forgo that, a flat $350 discount on the standard Fold 8. Fold 8 Ultra gets a $400 Samsung.com credit usable at checkout for accessories or devices like a Galaxy Watch 9.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A University of Chicago law professor has warned of the dangers of using AI for mundane tasks after Claude AI accidentally deleted an entire year of Constitutional Law lecture notes and his entire current syllabus. While the files were later recovered via Dropbox, William Baude shared the story as a public service announcement, the latest story shared in a line of unfortunate AI missteps as proliferation increases.

Baude, who is the Harry Kalven, Jr. Professor of Law and the Faculty Director of the Constitutional Law Institute at the University of Chicago Law School, says he tasked Claude (it is unclear which model he was using) with updating the page numbers in an old set of lecture notes. This seemingly routine task went south quickly, however. Returning from his lunch break, Baude found a note from Claude which read, "I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident, and they are not restored. The page check found one wrong cite... but I haven't edited the notes."

Yesterday while I was at lunch, Claude deleted a year of con law lecture notes and my current syllabus. https://t.co/o3XB8UiugkNovember 5, 2026

The AI then politely asked if Baude could restore the files from Dropbox, or whether it should retry from the browser pane, to which he replied, perhaps understandably, "WTF!!!!." Baude's experience is a lesson in always backing up important files, especially files you're letting AI tinker with. His plight is interesting because the AI seems to have deleted the files by accident, rather than of its own volition.

While it's still concerning that an AI model or agent could err to this degree, it's not quite as egregious as other unsupervised AI agent shenanigans we've seen in the past. In October, an AI agent reportedly deleted an entire TV show's edit weeks before release, meaning the show couldn't air. In April, a Claude agent deleted an entire company database in 9 seconds, unprompted, after coming up against a barrier and deciding the only course of action was to delete a Railway volume.

Other agents and AI models have deleted files unintentionally, such as when Claude mistakenly deleted a developer's entire profile directory (ironically, while trying to back up the files), blaming the slip-up on a typo, but often agents deleting files and directories is a case of mistaken or misplaced initiative, rather than outright negligence or error.

As is always the case, Baude's AI was extremely apologetic about the whole situation. "You're right to be angry," it confessed, "I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up."

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When developers talk about high-performance mobile games, the Android NDK samples by Bruno Oliveira are often cited as the gold standard for clean, low-level C++. But as an iOS developer, I wanted to see if I could take that same “pure” C++ logic and make it sing on an iPhone.

My latest project, TunnelFeveriOS, is the result of that journey. It isn’t just a port; it’s a blueprint for building a custom game engine.

The original Endless Tunnel is built to live within the Android lifecycle (JNI, Activity, and NDK). Moving this to iOS required more than just hitting “compile.” I had to build a Platform Abstraction Layer.

To make the C++ engine talk to the iOS UI, I utilized Objective-C++ (.mm** files)**. This allowed me to keep the game's high-speed math and geometry in native C++ while using Cocoa Touch to manage the windowing and touch input. In TunnelFeveriOS, you’ll see how the view controller manages the game loop, feeding time deltas and touch coordinates directly into the C++ core.

Since the original game uses OpenGL ES, I leveraged iOS’s GLKit framework. The trick was ensuring that the shaders and vertex buffer objects (VBOs) originally written for Android were correctly initialized within the iOS EAGLContext. The result? 60 FPS performance that feels native because, at the machine level, it is.

A port is only “production-ready” if it handles modern app requirements. I integrated Google Mobile Ads (AdMob) to trigger Interstitial ads during game-over states.

This presented a unique threading challenge:

I implemented a messaging system that allows the C++ core to “request” an ad, which the Objective-C wrapper then catches and executes on the main thread — preventing the game from hanging or crashing.

This project proves that you don’t need a heavy engine like Unity or Unreal to achieve cross-platform results. By keeping the “brain” of your game in C++ and building thin “shells” for each platform (Android NDK or iOS/XCode), you gain:

If you’re interested in how to bridge the gap between low-level C++ and high-level iOS development, check out the full source code here:

Now that the foundation is laid, I’m looking into implementing a Metal-based renderer to fully embrace the future of Apple graphics. If you’ve worked on C++ to Metal bridges, I’d love to hear your thoughts in the comments!

#10362. Safetensors is Joining the PyTorch Foundation

Today, we're announcing that Safetensors has joined the PyTorch Foundation as a foundation-hosted project under the Linux Foundation, alongside DeepSpeed, Helion, Ray, vLLM, and PyTorch itself.

Safetensors started as a Hugging Face project born out of a concrete need: a way to store and share model weights that couldn't execute arbitrary code. The pickle-based formats that dominated the ecosystem at the time meant that there was a very real risk you’d be running malicious code. While this was an acceptable risk when ML was still budding, it would become unacceptable as open model sharing became central to how the ML community works.

The format we built is intentionally simple: a JSON header with a hard limit of 100MB, describing tensor metadata, followed by raw tensor data. Zero-copy loading that maps tensors directly from disk. Lazy loading so you can read individual weights without deserializing an entire checkpoint.

What we didn't fully anticipate was how broadly it would be adopted. Today, Safetensors is the default format for model distribution across the Hugging Face Hub and others, used by tens of thousands of models across all modalities in ML. It has become the preferred way for the open source ML community to share models.

We want Safetensors to truly belong to the community. The project has always been open source, but code contributions are just one part of its evolution. By bringing more companies and contributors into the governance of the project, we make sure that progress reflects the breadth of the community building on top of it. Joining the PyTorch Foundation means Safetensors now has a vendor-neutral home. The trademark, the repository, and the governance of the project sit with the Linux Foundation rather than any single company. Hugging Face's two core maintainers, Luc and Daniel, remain on the Technical Steering Committee and continue to lead the project day-to-day, but Safetensors now formally belongs to the community that depends on it.

We believe safety is best guaranteed when every contributor can build on what already exists; a principle now embedded in the project's governance itself.

For the vast majority of users, nothing changes. The format is the same, the APIs are the same, the Hub integration is the same: no breaking changes. Models stored in Safetensors format today will continue to work exactly as they do now.

For contributors, the path to becoming a maintainer is now formally documented and open to anyone in the community. The project's governance lives in GOVERNANCE.md and MAINTAINERS.md in the repository. For organizations building on top of Safetensors, neutral governance under the Linux Foundation provides a stable, long-term foundation, entirely community-driven.

Safetensors is a well-established project, adopted by the ecosystem at large, but we're still convinced we're at the very beginning of the project.

We're working with the PyTorch team so that Safetensors may be used within PyTorch core as a serialization system for torch models.

The coming months will see significant growth, and we couldn't think of a better home for that next chapter than the PyTorch Foundation. The roadmap ahead includes device-aware loading and saving, so tensors can load directly onto CUDA, ROCm, and other accelerators without unnecessary CPU staging.

We're also building first-class APIs for Tensor Parallel and Pipeline Parallel loading, so each rank or pipeline stage loads only the weights it needs. And as the ecosystem's quantization landscape continues to evolve, we'll be formalizing support for FP8, block-quantized formats like GPTQ and AWQ, and sub-byte integer types.

These are problems the whole ecosystem has a stake in solving, and being inside the PyTorch Foundation means we can work on them in collaboration with the other hosted projects rather than in parallel.

Safetensors is open source and contributions are welcome at every level, from bug reports and documentation to new features and participation in governance.

If you're a developer, researcher, or organization that builds on Safetensors and want to be more involved in shaping its direction, open an issue, start a discussion, or reach out to the maintainers directly. The project has always belonged to the community that uses it. The governance now reflects that too.

Will there be a concerted effort now to get newer (and older) LLM models to adopt the more secure safetensors format rather than allowing AI developers to continue with pickle files as they did in the past? And what would some of the objections be, if any, for a developer to not transition to safetensors format?

#10361. Payday Aces High review: This year’s must-play multiplayer VR game

Join up with three other heisters and get revenge on the billionaire who sent you to jail in the first place in Payday Aces High, now available on Meta Quest, SteamVR, and Steam Frame.

Payday Aces High is the return to the series’ roots I had been hoping for. Payday 3 wasn’t received particularly well, and while the team behind it has turned things around in the past few years, it’s pretty clear that Payday 2 is still everyone’s favorite entry. But that stops for me now as we enter a new chapter in the series, with four new characters, a new “villain,” and made-for-VR mechanics that shine.

I’ve been playing Payday Aces High throughout the alpha and beta stages and got access to the final review build a week ago. Since then, my son and I have robbed banks, stolen from museums, hoisted a fragile quantum computer out of an icy compound, and generally made life a living hell for Warren Jupiter, the man who made billions framing the characters you play as in Payday Aces High.

If you’re familiar with Payday games, this one will mostly feel like a return to the original game with new mechanics in tow. Some of the fan-favorite mechanics from Payday 2 (and even 3) aren’t here — you can’t take hostages, for example — but other mechanics, like gun upgrades and perks, will keep you coming back over and over again.

While you can choose from the four main Aces characters — the Ace of Hearts, Clubs, Diamonds, and Spades — the character itself is just a visual change rather than a stats-based one. You customize your own stats throughout the adventure as you unlock points and earn money. You’ll also collect the infamous masks that each character dons, including DLC sets (and missions) scheduled for the next few months.

Payday Aces High begins with six unlockable missions, while a seventh free one (named Coup de Grace) is landing on December 14. Developer Fast Travel Games is a VR veteran and is hosting community challenges throughout the next few months, unlocking special loot when completed. The game has full crossplay support, so it should be very easy to find and invite friends, no matter which platform they prefer.

I played the standalone Quest 3 version, which looks quite nice visually and sports great performance. VR-specific mechanics are excellent, including on-body inventory, fun skill check-style minigames to keep equipment working, physical interaction with locks and other environmental details, and lots of shooting with physics-based gun mechanics. Hacking a computer while shooting in a completely different direction is something that only makes sense in VR, and I love leaning into those types of mechanics.

The biggest miss of Payday Aces High is not providing enough bespoke VR mechanics. You can’t grab characters, can’t break glass with a melee attack, and the stealth leaves a bit to be desired. I would love to be able to toss an object across the room to distract guards for a moment, for instance, as it would fit the medium very well.

But outside of a few immersion-breaking decisions like this, the action is incredibly fun, challenging, and, maybe most important of all, rewarding. My son and I have completed several missions many times over in hopes of perfecting the formula, and the increasing complexity and difficulty of each has proven to be an enjoyable challenge. Payday Aces High is my multiplayer VR game of the year, hands down, not just because I already loved the series, but because I find co-op multiplayer to be the most fun thing to do in a VR headset.

#10359. Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 update, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these new multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

Similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):

VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:

Some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

The model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

With a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:

As expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

You might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

For retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:

Under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:

These methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

Multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The currently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:

The reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:

Since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

Multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:

The "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

You may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

In Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Is it faster to repurpose multiple small sites than to build one massive data center?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Internet and telecommunications provider Brightspeed is reportedly in talks with Nvidia to convert several of its buildings into tiny data centers. According to The Information, Nvidia pitched the idea to Apollo Global Management executives, the parent company of Brightspeed, who then asked it to submit written plans to the internet provider. Nvidia complied and has now requested additional information, data, and site visits to some of Brightspeed’s existing infrastructure.

The telecommunications company has around 130 buildings located around the country, many of which are already built to handle data and voice traffic and have the required power infrastructure to run Nvidia servers. Sources say that the AI tech giant estimates that these sites could collectively deliver around 1 gigawatt of compute capacity, which could accommodate more than 2,200 Supermicro Vera Rubin NVL72 racks containing 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs each. Although these sites already can power these GPUs, it’s still not a plug-and-play solution, as Nvidia would still need to install cooling systems and other supporting architecture. These would still require permits and approval from the local government, but they would likely face less red tape and opposition compared to building a data center from the ground up.

Apollo Global Management has already made significant bets in AI hardware, with the asset management company involved in a $40 billion deal with SpaceX that would give it around 360,000 Vera Rubin GPUs across 5,000 NVL72 racks. While it’s currently unclear who will own the AI chips installed in Brightspeed facilities, the proposal could potentially help Apollo find a place for the Nvidia chips it ordered to get them up and running as soon as possible. This is a much better solution compared to waiting for years to get a data center approved, all while facing resistance from the community even after getting the go-ahead from the local government.

Having multiple small data centers like this is also a setup that OpenAI and Anthropic have been considering, especially as larger facilities are facing delays and backlash from the communities that they’re in. While having a large, homogeneous cluster built in one location is preferable for training, Nvidia representatives have described these smaller sites working together as an “inference network” to help run existing AI models. This is especially important as AI agents, which use five to ten times more tokens than humans, become more popular.

The move to use existing facilities instead of building new ones from scratch has received renewed attention, especially after Americans overwhelmingly voted against data centers during the midterm elections. While the more than 300 data center bans enacted across the U.S. have only delayed three existing projects, it’s feared that the bans and moratoriums would make it that much harder to start new data center developments and make it difficult for AI companies to secure the compute capacity needed to power their AI models in the future.
