#10355. How Product Teams Can Use AI User Research to Test Assumptions Before Sprint Planning

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sprint planning is on Thursday, and the top of the backlog rests on three things nobody has checked. Users want the feature, they will find it, and they will understand what it does when they do. Each belief is plausible, and each has already been written into a ticket.

AI user research uses language models to simulate or analyze user conversations, so a team can put a question to a modeled audience in minutes instead of recruiting people for weeks. Used well, it gives a product team a cheap first check on backlog assumptions. Used badly, it produces confident-sounding agreement. This guide covers a two-day routine that gets the benefit and avoids the trap.

An assumption is worth testing when the plan depends on it and a wrong answer would change the ticket. "Users like clean interfaces" fails that test. "Analysts re-apply the same filters every session" passes, because if it is false the saved-filters feature shrinks or disappears.

The timing matters because planning leaves little room for research. The Scrum Guide says Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and the first question the team answers is why the Sprint is valuable. Checks run before that meeting inform the answer. Checks run during it eat the time meant for deciding.

Write each risky item as a short card that names the belief, the consequence of being wrong, and the decision it feeds. A card forces the team to say what would change its mind, which most tickets never do. Here is an example:

Aim for three to five cards. A team that tries to test the whole backlog will test none of it, and the cards on the riskiest items give the best return.

AI user research comes in two forms. The first analyzes data you already hold: clustering support tickets and summarizing interview transcripts. It works on real evidence, so its main risk is a sloppy summary.

The second form interviews simulated people. AI user research of this kind builds a panel of modeled personas matched to your target profile, asks them your questions, and reports the themes. It needs no recruiting and returns results quickly, which fits a two-day window. Its output comes from a model of users and not from users, and that distinction should appear in every planning document that cites it.

A simulated audience helps most when you want to sharpen a question, and least when you need proof. Nielsen Norman Group's 2024 review of synthetic users found them useful for generating hypotheses and preparing interview guides. It warned against using them for final decisions or concept validation, and for niche populations, because AI tends to please and "every idea is often seen as a good one."

Spend Tuesday collecting answers and Wednesday reading them skeptically. On Tuesday, put each card's question to the modeled audience in neutral wording, and ask what would make them not use the feature. A question phrased as "Would saved filters help you?" invites a yes, while "Walk me through setting up your weekly report" does not.

On Wednesday, compare the answers with what you already know from support tickets and analytics. Mark each assumption as supported, contradicted, or unclear. Treat a unanimous answer with suspicion, because real audiences rarely agree on anything. Also be wary of lists in which the modeled users "seem to care about everything," which is how Nielsen Norman Group describes their weak prioritization.

Whatever stays unclear or high risk goes to real people. Jakob Nielsen's classic analysis found that five users find about 85% of usability problems, assuming comparable users, and he recommended several small rounds over one large one. An AI check is a good way to decide what those five people should be asked.

Each mark maps to a different decision. A contradicted assumption means the ticket is cut or reduced to its smallest useful version. A supported assumption that rests only on simulated evidence is not yet safe, so schedule a real-user check as the first task in the sprint, ahead of the build work that depends on it. An unclear assumption should not receive full scope.

The cost of skipping this step is real. A 2019 analysis of 615 product subscriptions by a product analytics vendor found that about 12% of features generate 80% of daily usage volume, and 80% of features are rarely or never used. That is one vendor's customer base, and the figures cover features that customers chose to track, so treat them as a rough guide. They still suggest that most of a backlog is a bet.

AI user research cannot replace talking to real users. Nielsen Norman Group found that synthetic users gave overly optimistic accounts of their own behavior, such as claiming to finish every course in a study, and that they cannot supply real past experience. It also called presenting synthetic findings as real-user findings "an unethical way to share what you've learned."

Two habits keep a team honest. Label every piece of evidence in the planning document as modeled, observed, or reported, and require that any feature built on modeled evidence has a real-user check scheduled. The review also warned that teams starting with synthetic research may get comfortable and skip the real kind, so put the real check on the calendar before the first AI result arrives.

Can AI user research replace interviews with real users? No. It is a cheap first pass that helps you write better questions and spot weak assumptions. Anything that drives a significant build still needs real people.

How many assumptions should a team test before planning? Three to five. Pick the ones where a wrong answer would cut or reshape a ticket.

How do I stop simulated users from just agreeing with me? Use neutral, open questions, ask what would make them avoid the feature, and treat unanimous answers as a warning sign.

What should I do with results I cannot verify? Mark them as modeled, give them less weight than observed evidence, and schedule a real-user check before committing full scope.

Sources: Scrum Guide, Sprint Planning; Jakob Nielsen, "Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users" (March 18, 2000); Nielsen Norman Group, "Synthetic Users: If, When, and How to Use AI-Generated 'Research'" (June 21, 2024); 2019 Feature Adoption Report (615 product subscriptions, vendor-reported).

#10354. Three layers, one repo: a tour of google/adk-recipes

A developer building on Google Cloud today can scaffold a long-horizon memory agent from the terminal, install a retail vertical skill into a coding assistant with one line, and deploy a fully-wired production service to Cloud Run, Agent Runtime, Agent Garden, or Gemini Enterprise app — all from the same curated source tree. That tree is google/adk-recipes, the restructured successor to google/adk-samples that now serves Agent Platform from a single source of truth.

ADK recipes are agent-friendly: we've made it easy for your agents to 1) discover relevant recipes for various agent use cases, and 2) install and use them automatically from your favorite harness.

google/adk-recipes splits its content into three top-level folders: core/ for reference patterns curated by the Agents CLI and DevRel teams, plugins/ for installable vertical skills packaged as Plugin Recipes conforming to the Agent Plugins v1.0.0 spec, and contrib/ for end-to-end deployable services across five languages. Every piece has been designed with machine readability as the primary consideration.

What follows is a walkthrough of the repository's shape, three worked examples (one per layer), and a reflection on what the new structure enables.

Three top-level roots, each anchored on one reader action:

Every recipe ships a validated manifest.yaml, an AGENTS.md that tells the coding assistant opening it what the recipe is and how to use it, and (for contrib/ and plugins/) a Dockerfile plus a runnability test. CI enforces the standards on every PR, and a suite of coding-assistant skills in the repo (prepare-python-recipe, generate-manifest, github-pr-review, and others) does most of the preparation, so your agent can scaffold, validate, and submit a recipe end-to-end.

Every AGENTS.md, every manifest.yaml, every SKILL.md is written primarily for the AI coding assistant that will open the repo on your behalf; README.md files are what humans still read. The handbook glossary captures the dual framing: "Recipe — a runnable agent example (or importable agent module) under core/, contrib/, or plugins/, consumed by ADK developers and coding agents alike."

adk-recipes serves as the single source of truth for ADK content across the three Agent Platform surfaces that consume it. Each reads the repository through its own protocol.

Agents CLI reads core/. When a developer runs uvx --from google-agents-cli agents-cli create my-agent, Agents CLI can scaffold on demand a core/ recipe. The CLI, launched earlier this year at Google Cloud Next, exposes the full scaffold → deploy → evaluate → publish lifecycle; the base content it serves comes from our recipes. Horizon, the reference harness we examine below, is an example pattern Agents CLI treats as a production template.

Agent Garden features a curated selection. The developer-facing path into the repository is a pull request to contrib/: a recipe lands in GitHub, becomes part of the public ADK ecosystem, and from that moment is discoverable by other developers and by coding assistants reading the repository. Appearing in the Agent Garden gallery is a separate editorial decision made by the Agent Garden team, which curates a subset of recipes and promotes them to the public catalog on their own cadence. Once an agent is in the gallery, any developer in a Google Cloud project gets a one-click install.

Beyond these primary surfaces, Google Cloud's own infrastructure components appear as building blocks inside the recipes themselves. Horizon uses Agent Platform Sandboxes for per-user sandboxing, Memory Bank for durable memory, and Agent Platform Sessions for session state. The retail product-search Plugin Recipe uses Vector Search 2.0 on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform paired with BigQuery. The retail virtual-tryon Plugin Recipe uses Gemini image models for still composites and Veo 3.1 Reference-to-Video for animated outputs. The recipes do not just live alongside Agent Platform; they document it in use.

For developers working with coding assistants outside Google Cloud's tooling (Claude Code, Antigravity, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, and others), Plugin Recipes additionally install through the open npx skills CLI maintained by vercel-labs.

Building an agent that can handle a single conversation is a well-understood problem. Building one that holds its own across days of interaction, remembering what the user did yesterday and planning tasks for tomorrow, is a materially different undertaking. The hard parts of such a long-horizon system are the same regardless of what the agent is being built to do: cross-session memory, per-user sandboxing of tool execution, secrets management, guardrails against runaway behaviour, and the orchestration primitives that make multi-step tasks resumable. Horizon, which lives at core/python/long-horizon-harness, is the reference harness we built to collect these primitives in one place.

The shortest path from a fresh clone to a running Horizon instance:

make deploy rolls the backend to Cloud Run through Terraform; make destroy tears it back down. Horizon's evaluation suite lives in tests/eval/evalsets/ as eighteen named behavioural rubrics covering memory recall, injection-based exfiltration attempts, guardrail halting under adversarial input, tool-selection discipline, and a journey-level plot-artifact evaluation. The rubrics are executed with uv run pytest tests/eval.

A first chat turn against the running backend confirms the memory layer is wired correctly:

Horizon is the harness we give coding assistants to study before building something harder. When a developer asks their assistant to build an agent that must run across days of interaction, the right next step is uvx google-agents-cli create with Horizon as the scaffold, and the rest of the harness falls into place.

Horizon encodes a reference pattern. It does not encode a vertical. For that, the second layer of the repository holds Plugin Recipes, each addressing a specific industry domain. The first vertical fully covered in this launch is retail, available under plugins/retail/.

The Plugin Recipe format sits on top of the Agent Plugins v1.0.0 specification published at agent-plugins.org, an open standard for packaging installable AI skills across coding assistants. The specification defines a plugin as a bundle of one or more skills with a top-level plugin.json manifest declaring name, version, license, and ownership. Each skill is a self-contained folder with a SKILL.md conversational installer, a README.md, an EVAL.yaml of quality gates, and the scripts and assets the skill needs to do its work. The retail plugin's layout is:

Two skills ship in this plugin today. The first, retail-product-search, builds an ADK agent with a vector-search retrieval tool backed by Vector Search 2.0 on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and a BigQuery catalog. The skill handles the entire pipeline: ingesting a CSV or JSON catalog into BigQuery, generating multimodal and text embeddings with Vertex AI Embeddings, building the Vector Search collection, scaffolding the ADK agent with a retrieve_docs tool, and deploying to Cloud Run. The agent is deliberately single-agent: one root_agent with one retrieval tool and no coordinator layer. The semantic complexity sits in the retrieval pipeline and the evaluator rubric, not in agent-to-agent communication; adding orchestration layers would obscure the pattern rather than clarify it.

The second skill, retail-virtual-tryon, generates a photorealistic composite of a model wearing or holding a product, with an optional eight-second studio catwalk video on top. It uses gemini-2.5-flash-image by default, falling back to gemini-2.5-pro-image when editorial quality matters more than latency. For video it uses veo-3.1-generate-001 in Reference-to-Video mode, conditioning the generated motion on the still produced by the image pipeline. The skill ships a pre-flight product-cutout classifier and configurable safety levels, operational details that become obvious after the third real production deployment.

Both skills install into any coding assistant that reads skills with a single command:

The --full-depth flag instructs the CLI to walk past its default top-level lookup and discover the nested plugins/retail/skills/ structure. The install lands in ~/.agents/skills// and is symlinked into every detected coding assistant on the local machine:

The skill ecosystem is designed to compose. The retail-product-search SKILL.md instructs the host coding assistant to pull two companion skills from google/skills if they are not already installed, keeping cross-cutting concerns like BigQuery basics and Gemini API usage in one place and reusable by multiple vertical plugins.

Once installed, the coding assistant reads SKILL.md and initiates a Q-MODE interview. For retail-product-search, Quick Start is two questions (GCP project ID and the path to product data, with sensible defaults for both); Full Setup adds two more covering product-fields level and GCP region. By the end of the interview the skill has written a ./design-spec.md reflecting the project's actual shape and executed scripts/setup.py to land the catalog in BigQuery, generate the embeddings, build the Vector Search collection, and run EVAL.yaml against the result. If the rubric and assertion checks fall below the 80 percent passing target, the skill halts and surfaces the specific failures.

An end-to-end setup run on the bundled five-product demo catalog produces:

A live retrieval against the collection the skill has just provisioned returns:

The virtual-tryon skill is faster to demonstrate interactively. A direct call to generate_tryon_image with a user portrait and a product image produces the photorealistic composite shown at the top of this section in roughly ten seconds. The same inputs piped through generate_tryon_video and Veo Reference-to-Video turn that still into an eight-second studio catwalk animation of the composite in motion.

The pipeline is category-agnostic. Swapping the product image for a pair of sunglasses, with product_category='eyewear', invokes the same generate_tryon_image call and produces a composite in the correct category without any further configuration:

Retail is the first vertical fully covered in this format. Additional verticals will land as their own folders under plugins/, following the same anatomy and the same Agent Plugins specification, so developers can expect a consistent install experience across industries.

The contrib/ layer is where ADK recipes become end-to-end deployable services. Twelve Python agents live there today, spanning the kinds of applications ADK is typically used to build in practice: finance (financial advisor, small-business loan processor), evaluation (LLM auditor), document and knowledge pipelines (high-volume document analyzer, multiformat hybrid RAG), content and brand (brand-aligned presentations, brand-search optimization, on-brand genmedia), retail (product search, virtual try-on), and framework examples (agent-skills tutorial, staged UI widgets). Java, Go, TypeScript, and Kotlin each carry smaller sets. Every entry in contrib/ is a worked example of how a core/ pattern or a plugins/ skill becomes a running service.

To make the relationship between a plugin and its deployable counterpart concrete, take contrib/python/retail-product-search as the example. The retail plugin from the previous section walked a developer through a conversational install that provisioned the Vector Search collection, the BigQuery catalog, and the embeddings. The contrib agent is the deployable counterpart: a long-running service that reads from that collection and answers natural-language shopping queries over it. The plugin owns the one-shot setup; the contrib agent owns the service shape. Both are maintained by the same team to stay synchronised, and the agent's README directs new users to run the plugin's setup first:

Once the collection (retail-skill-products-collection) is populated, the agent is cloned out of contrib/python/retail-product-search, pointed at a GCP project, and surfaced on one of five deployment personas controlled by boolean flags in .env.

Once the deployment is live, the agent exposes a hosted shopping-assistant endpoint. The same retrieve_docs tool we called directly from Python now sits behind a chat interface, reachable through the deployed Reasoning Engine or, during development, through the ADK Web UI. The exact same agent code answering the exact same shopping query, run locally for inspection:

The agent graph on the left of the UI confirms the single-agent architecture (product_search_agent → retrieve_docs). The right panel traces each tool invocation. The response grounds in a real catalog row from Vector Search: "Sony Wireless Headphones · Price: $199.99 · Brand: Sony · Rating: 4.5/5 (50 in stock) · Premium noise-cancelling over-ear headphones featuring an impressive 30-hour battery life." No products are hallucinated; the Vector Search collection on top of BigQuery is the source of truth.

That is what the retail plugin gives a team. The plugin encodes the data-pipeline setup once, through a conversational install any coding assistant can execute. The contrib agent is the running service, deployable in five shapes, that any organisation can take as a starting point and swap in its own catalog. The virtual-tryon counterpart in contrib/python/retail-virtual-tryon follows the same pattern: a smaller root agent that orchestrates try_on_product_image and try_on_product_video tools, deployable in the same five shapes, built on the virtual-tryon plugin's one-shot setup.

A reference harness without a vertical is a toy; a vertical skill without a deployable artifact is a slide; a deployable agent without a reference pattern is a prototype no one can repeat. Shipping all three in one repository, under a shared manifest schema and governance pipeline, lets a developer or a coding assistant walk the stack in either direction, with every Agent Platform surface reading from the same source of truth.

The practical result is a lower barrier from "I need an agent that does X" to a running production service: a coding assistant can scaffold a Horizon-shaped agent, install a vertical Plugin Recipe, and reach the deployment transcripts in contrib/ without translating between repositories or reconciling manifest formats. For teams building vertical solutions, Plugin Recipes package domain expertise once and distribute it to every coding assistant on the market with the same install flow and quality gates.

Not an officially supported Google product. Recipes are for demonstration and as starting points, not production use.

Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels

Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats

Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services

#10353. Waypoint-1.5: Higher-Fidelity Interactive Worlds for Everyday GPUs

Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.

The first release of Waypoint showed that real-time generative worlds were possible. It proved that interactive world models could be more than passive video demos, and that locally runnable systems could begin to close the gap between generating a world and actually stepping into one.

Waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation. This release improves visual fidelity, expands the range of hardware that can run the model locally, and takes another step toward interactive world simulation without datacenter-scale compute.

On desktop hardware including RTX 3090 through 5090, Waypoint-1.5 can generate real-time environments at up to 720p and 60 FPS. This release also introduces a 360p tier designed to run smoothly across a much broader range of consumer hardware, including gaming laptops, and (soon) Apple Silicon Macs.

The biggest change in Waypoint-1.5 is accessibility.

With Waypoint-1, we proved the core experience. With Waypoint-1.5, we wanted to make that experience available on more machines without giving up real-time interactivity. That meant building two model tiers: a 720p model for higher-performance hardware, and a 360p model optimized for broader deployment.

We also scaled training dramatically. Waypoint-1.5 was trained on nearly 100x more data than Waypoint-1, which significantly improves the model’s ability to generate more coherent environments and more consistent motion over time.

Under the hood, Waypoint-1.5 also incorporates more efficient video modeling techniques to reduce redundant computation across frames. That matters because real-time world models are not judged only by how a single frame looks. They are judged by whether the world responds instantly, stays coherent as you move through it, and remains usable on local hardware.

A lot of recent progress in generative video and world models has focused on visual fidelity. Those results matter, but fidelity alone is not what makes an interactive world feel real.

What people remember is responsiveness. They remember whether the environment reacts to them, whether motion stays coherent, whether the world holds together as they explore it, and whether the whole experience feels immediate instead of delayed.

That is the gap we care about most: the difference between watching a generated scene and actually being inside one.

If world models only run on large GPU clusters, they remain impressive demos. If they run locally on consumer hardware, they become something much more useful: a foundation for interactive entertainment, creative tooling, simulation, and AI-native environments people can actually explore.

Waypoint-1.5 is designed around that idea: not just better videos, but more responsive and explorable worlds that remain accessible on consumer hardware.

The first is local execution through Overworld Biome. This release is designed to run across a wide range of hardware configurations, and the updated Biome runtime makes local setup much simpler. With the new installer flow, users can go from download to running the model locally in minutes.

The second is Overworld Stream, which lets you try Waypoint-1.5 instantly in the browser with no local setup required.

Whether you want immediate access or full local control, Waypoint-1.5 is built to support both.

Additionally, we provide World Engine, our flexible, easy to use, core inference library powering our official clients, along with nearly a dozen third party clients and libraries.

Waypoint started with a simple question: what would it take for generative worlds to become truly interactive?

Early generative systems showed that models could produce convincing images and videos. But building environments that people can explore, control, and interact with in real time is a different challenge entirely.

Waypoint-1.5 is another step in that direction, improving fidelity and expanding hardware accessibility while continuing to push real-time interactive generation onto local machines.

We think the future of world models will not be defined only by what they can render, but by whether people can actually inhabit and interact with them in real time.

Download Waypoint-1.5, run it locally with Biome, or jump in instantly on Overworld.stream.

And if you build something fun, strange, or unexpectedly immersive with it, we’d love to see it.

#10352. Oppo confirms its next foldable will actually know what a ‘global’ release is

The Oppo Find N6 is a stunning foldable but, for the second year in a row, it really stretches the definition of what a “global” release means. Oppo Find N7, apparently, will fix that.

Oppo Find N5 and Find N6 both saw global launches, but the company’s definition of that excluded Europe and virtually every other major market. For the most part, both foldables were essentially sold only in China, with major markets elsewhere left out. And that’s a shame, because both raised the bar for foldables in major ways.

Now, we’re looking forward to the launch of Oppo Find N7, a device rumored to be adopting the wide form factor popularized by Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, and that Oppo technically offered before anyone else.

And it might actually get a global release.

Speaking to Nixanbal (via GSMArena), Oppo apparently confirmed that its next foldable will see a release in Europe. It’d be the first time an Oppo foldable made its way to the region, with the OnePlus Open serving as Oppo’s global foldable back in 2023 for its one and only generation.

As for a release date, that’s still unconfirmed, but Oppo tends to release new foldables early in the year, so March 2027, give or take, is probably when we’ll see more officially.

#10351. I bought the knock-off Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air bands, and it’s crazy how good they are [Gallery]

I love swapping out the bands on my Pixel Watch 5 and Fitbit Air, but Google’s official options are not cheap. It doesn’t take long to find a plethora of knock-off Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air bands around the web and, as it turns out, they’re actually really good.

Over the past few generations, I’ve collected a ton of Pixel Watch bands and, at first, that was almost entirely first-party bands. For the first couple of years of Pixel Watch, third-party bands were either non-existent or of terrible quality, but they’ve gotten a lot better.

Last year, I showcased some knock-off Active Sport bands that, for $8, very effectively filled the gap for me while Google’s lineup was lacking some colors I wanted.

Since then, I’ve tried others. The most recent batch is a 6-pack of Pixel Watch bands that are copies of Google’s standard “Active” band. They’re made from silicone, not the fluorelastomer from past generations, nor the “Hydrogenated Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (HNBR)” used on Pixel Watch 5. But, in action, it gets the job done.

The bands sit somewhere between Google’s small and large sizes and slot into the Pixel Watch 5’s mechanism perfectly. If you handed this to me and said it was an official band from Google, I’d probably believe you.

To get this level of quality at such a low price is wild, all while getting colors that, again, Google doesn’t make. I found this while just wanting a purple band, but the price tag pushed me to just buy a whole pack, and the striking deep red included sneakily became one of my favorites.

Pixel Watch isn’t alone here – third-party knock-off bands for Fitbit Air are very good, as my colleage Damien Wilde has pointed out repeatedly.

I originally bought the Stephen Curry edition Fitbit Air and, long story short, I don’t have that official band anymore. But the $9 (currently even cheaper!) knock-off I bought on Amazon is quite literally identical in quality, feel, and even the details. The only thing it’s missing is the Stephen Curry badge (which, frankly, I don’t miss anyway), but it still has that little piece of added material where the wordmark would have been.

The same goes for the matching band I picked up for my Pixel Watch 5.

Google doesn’t sell this band on its own, which is annoying, but the knock-off I bought is basically identical to what I felt during our hands-on with the official one back in August, though this one doesn’t have the space for the Stephen Curry badge the real one does. The lugs connecting to the watch are also different and not nearly as stylish, but I’m absolutely not complaining here.

Is it possible that Google’s supply chain is producing these near-identical versions? Given the quality at play, I really wouldn’t be surprised! That said, a lot of these are simple copies. It’s not all that hard to spin up generic versions of products like these.

Most third party cheap Fitbit Air bands I've tried range from "decent" to "very good".

Most third party cheap and expensive Pixel Watch bands I've tried range from "very, very bad" to "almost decent".

The major issue with PW 3rd party bands isn't the band itself. It's the connecting lugs.

Not how they look, but how they're manufactured. High tolerances, rattling, too lose or too tight connections.

And that applies also to certified "made for Google" bands (i.e. the Spigen ones).

I've given up. I'm going to buy the official Pixel Watch leather band and take the official lugs out of it, so I can use with any 22mm strap.

I’ll still happily pick up some of Google’s official bands because it’s hard to beat some of those color options but, for the most part, it’s getting hard to go wrong with the knock-off Pixel Watch bands, and even more so with the Fitbit Air. The simpler tracker gets even better third-party options seeing as Google made the mounting mechanism free for everyone.

Whatever the case, third-party / knock-off Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air bands are in a really good place right now, and that’s refreshing after a few years of using this lineup every day.

#10350. Meet HoloTab by HCompany. Your AI browser companion.

We built one of the most powerful computer-use AIs in the world. And made it directly accessible from your browser. On March 31st, we released Holo3, our most advanced computer-use model to date.

Building something powerful is one thing; making it accessible and easy to use is another. We’re doing both.

HoloTab is a Chrome extension that navigates the web just like a person would. It automates tasks across any website with zero setup or technical skills required. You describe what you want, and the agent handles it directly inside your browser, navigating interfaces, filling fields, and making decisions the same way you would. The vision models, the action planning, the interface understanding, all of it is running underneath, working for you, and all you ever see is the result.

Some tasks are quick and forgettable, but others are long and repetitive, the kind that reliably eat up your afternoon. You might find yourself cross-referencing competitor pricing across twenty different e-commerce tabs to update a master spreadsheet, or filtering through a dozen job boards and company career pages to find new listings, painstakingly porting the details into a tracking doc to manage your applications.

That's where routines come in. You start a recording, and HoloTab captures what you do in your tab in real time while you click or narrate along the way, demonstrating what you're doing and why. Your screen and your actions give HoloTab everything it needs, enriching the routine with enough context to actually understand the goal.

Once the recording stops, a routine is generated. From then on, you can re-run your routine or schedule it whenever you need to, and HoloTab will handle the rest on its own.

Computer-use AI is going to change how people work, research, and get things done, both in their professional and personal lives, and that shift is already closer than most people realize. But it shouldn't require a technical background to access, and the benefits shouldn't accrue only to teams with engineers who know how to wire these systems together.

HoloTab is free and ready for everyone to use today: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/holotab/hlaoiikljjgcjdhkakedfngifaopbcop

#10347. Inside VAKRA: Reasoning, Tool Use, and Failure Modes of Agents

VAKRA Dataset | LeaderBoard | Release Blog | GitHub | Submit to Leaderboard

We recently introduced VAKRA, a tool-grounded, executable benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents reason and act in enterprise-like environments.

Unlike traditional benchmarks that test isolated skills, VAKRA measures compositional reasoning across APIs and documents, using full execution traces to assess whether agents can reliably complete multi-step workflows.

VAKRA provides an executable environment where agents interact with over 8,000+ locally hosted APIs backed by real databases spanning 62 domains, along with domain-aligned document collections. Tasks can require 3-7 step reasoning chains that combine structured API interaction with unstructured retrieval under natural-language tool-use constraints.

As can be seen below, models perform poorly on VAKRA - in this blog, we include additional dataset details about the tasks in VAKRA and present an analysis of failure modes we observed on different tasks.

As shown below, the VAKRA benchmark comprises of four tasks, each testing a different set of capabilities.

Fig 1: Representative examples of each capability in the VAKRA benchmark

This capability includes 2,077 test instances across 54 domains, requiring the use of tools from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD collections (Elder et al., 2026). Compared to the setup in Elder et al., the tool universe in SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD is expanded through the inclusion of a larger number of domains. Each domain is restricted to one tool collection, and tasks involve chaining 1–12 tool calls to arrive at the final answer.

Fig 2: Data sample from SEL-BIRD collection

As shown above, each instance has an associated JSON data source from which the answer must be derived. The MCP servers supporting this task include a special tool, called get_data(tool_universe_id=id), which must be called at the beginning of each instance. This tool initializes the data source, returns a lightweight preview of the data (see below Figure 3), and stores the full dataset server-side to avoid large data transfers. This prevents the inefficient transfer of large data over the MCP protocol. The call also configures the MCP server to expose the appropriate tool set based on the tool_universe_id and aligns the data source with the domain-specific database for the instance.

The SLOT-BIRD collection provides a global set of 7 tools for generic data manipulation (e.g., filtering, sorting), inspired by systems like Tableau and Google Analytics. The SEL-BIRD collection extends this by introducing more specialized tools: some are shared with SLOT-BIRD, while others are derived by flattening categorical arguments into separate functions (e.g., sort_data with argument ascending: bool = False becomes sort_data_ascending and sort_data_descending). Additionally, the generic (retrieve_data) function from SLOT-BIRD is replaced with query-specific getters. Every key in the data for a given instance has an associated get function (get_KEY_NAME) for an average of 4 get functions per instance.

Fig 3: Data preview obtained from `get_data` function

This capability includes 1,597 instances across 17 domains, requiring tools from an expanded REST-BIRD collection (Elder et al.). These use endpoint-style interfaces that provide highly specific, query-aligned endpoints that encapsulate most computation. They are served as REST APIs running in a FastAPI server, which is wrapped by the MCP server. This task requires selecting the correct APIs from the domain-specific tool set (as shown in the example in Figure 1). Each domain contains a minimum of 6 to a maximum of 328 tools (with an average of 116 tools). Similar to the previous task, the get_data tool configures the MCP server to expose only the relevant domain-specific APIs.

The OpenAI API Specification restricts the tool list input to a maximum length of 128 tools. This restriction requires an agent builder using this API to manage the length of the tool list directly via a shortlisting mechanism. In the baseline agents in our repository, a simple shortlisting capability handles this challenge.

The Capability 3 segment of the benchmark has 869 test instances drawn from 38 subject domains. These instances rely again on the REST-BIRD API collection, but add multi-hop reasoning to the challenge (refer to example in Figure 1). Multi-hop questions require multiple pieces of supporting evidence to be extracted and combined to reach an answer. The instances in this section require between one and five logical hops to answer a query. The question types distribution for queries within the test dataset is shown below in Figure 4.

Fig 4: API Hop-Type distribution for Capability 3 (MultiHop) and Hybrid Hop-Type distribution for Capability 4 (MultiHop MultiSource Reasoning)

Capability 4 includes 644 instances across 41 domains and is also built on the REST-BIRD API collection. Figure 4 above shows a distribution of hybrid hops for test queries without policies. It contains the most complex queries with the following characteristics:

Multi-Source: This segment adds document indices per domain. Queries in this capability could require information from these document indexes as well as API calls. Similar to Capability 3, this task also has Multi-Hop queries. The required information source applies at the per-hop level, so, for example, a question may entail three logical hops with sources: API - RAG (Document Retrieval) - API. To enforce correct reasoning, sources are decontaminated during data generation, i.e. information required for a given hop is available in only one source. For example, if a hop is to be answered using APIs, the document index is built by removing documents that likely contain the information needed to answer the question.

Multi-Turn: This segment of the dataset also adds multi-turn conversations to the setting. Each instance is a dialog with multiple turns. The data is released as context-response pairs, where the context encodes the current dialog history and the agent is only responsible for answering the current turn.

Tool-usage Policies: A subset of these instances includes tool-use policies that the agent is required to follow. These policies take the form of plain-text instructions about the knowledge sources that the agent is allowed to access and under which circumstances. For example:

The baseline agent in the project repo imposes adherence to these policies through a simple addition to the prompt: "You are a helpful assistant with access to tools.\n Tool Usage Constraint: {additional_instructions}.". Of course, agent builders are free to choose any constraint enforcement mechanism.

VAKRA evaluates agents in tool environments where success depends on both the ability to execute coherent, multi-step workflows and answer correctness. We introduce an execution-centric evaluation framework that assesses not only final outputs but also the full tool-execution trajectory that includes tool calls, inputs, and intermediate results.

The VAKRA Evaluator operates over two key inputs for each sample: a predicted final response and the corresponding tool-call trajectory. The tool calls from the predicted trajectory are executed in the same environment as the ground truth to verify intermediate tool outputs.

The evaluation follows a waterfall-style pipeline (Figure 6), where later stages are conditioned on earlier success:

Fig 6: Waterfall-style Evaluation Pipeline

Tool-Sequence Comparison Due to the presence of an executable environment, agents can explore the environment and sometimes return the answer by invoking a different set of APIs than the ones identified by us. In order to support alternative but valid tool invocations and reasoning paths, correctness is assessed by executing each predicted tool and comparing the set of tool responses against those from the ground truth (rather than enforcing strict step-level matching).

Specifically, we first perform a programmatic check, verifying whether all information present in the ground-truth tool responses is recovered by the predicted tool responses. This check may be inconclusive in cases involving partial matches, semantic equivalence, or differences in representation (e.g., ordering, aggregation, or formatting). In such cases, we apply a secondary LLM-based evaluation, adapted from the CRAG framework Yang et al., 2024, to determine whether the predicted trajectory retrieves all required information despite structural differences. This step uses an adapted prompt to determine whether the predicted trajectory captures all required information, even if obtained through a different sequence of tool calls.

Final Response Evaluation For trajectories that pass the previous check, the final response is evaluated using an LLM-based judge. This step ensures that the response is (i) grounded in the predicted tool outputs, and (ii) factually consistent with the ground truth answer, accounting for potential variations in phrasing or structure.

This design ensures that agents are rewarded not only for producing correct answers, but for obtaining them through valid and complete reasoning processes.

Every capability is equally weighted to obtain a final leaderboard score

To obtain a capability score, every sample within a capability is equally weighted for capabilities 1 through 3.

For capability 4, we weight heterogeneous queries higher:

We now present detailed error analysis across the four VAKRA capabilities. To facilitate our analysis, we adopt stage-wise error categorization to assign each failure to the first point of breakdown. Specifically, we evaluate, in order: (i) whether the correct tool(s) were selected, (ii) whether the required arguments were provided without omissions or hallucinations, (iii) whether argument values were correct, and (iv) whether the final response is both accurate and grounded in the tool outputs.

Since a single sample may exhibit multiple errors across different steps, we sequentially classify each instance to the earliest failing stage (e.g., tool selection errors take precedence over argument errors). This avoids double-counting and allows error categories to be interpreted as disjoint fractions of the dataset. While more granular metrics (e.g., precision/recall over tool usage) are possible (Elder et al., 2026), we find this formulation provides a simple and interpretable breakdown of agent failures.

The instances in this part of the benchmark required selecting and sequencing multiple tools to solve a single task. We have 2077 samples in this capability. This was challenging for all models, but GPT-OSS-120B performed best on this segment of the benchmark.

Fig 7: SEL-BIRD vs SLOT-BIRD Error Types Analysis

The Business Intelligence (BI) API capability contains two sets of APIs, from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD tool collections. The SEL part of this benchmark had 600 samples, while the SLOT part of the benchmark had 1477 samples. These two collections are grouped under the BI API capability, but have slightly different characteristics. The SLOT-BIRD collection has a smaller number of generic tools with a large number of parameter values to fill, while the SEL-BIRD collection has a larger set of tools and fewer parameters per tool. This focus is reflected in the relative errors made by models using these two tool collections.

Fig 8: Comparison of Accuracy Across Models by Hop Depth

Multi-hop reasoning increases the difficulty of the original task by requiring models to successfully answer multiple implicitly coupled questions, each of which requires selecting and calling the correct API. As expected, all models performed best on the questions with only a single logical hop, and saw performance degradations on 2-hop and again on 3+ hop questions.

Fig 9: Model Accuracy Rates by Interaction Type (API, Document-Retriever, Hybrid)

The final segment of the dataset includes document sources in addition to the tool/API sources in the other segments. This leads to instances that require single or multiple API calls, single or multiple document searches, or some combination of API calls and document searches.

Fig 10: Model Accuracy Rates by Policy Type

Policies introduce an additional layer of difficulty on top of multi-hop, multi-source reasoning. When policies align with the required source for answering i.e. they do not affect the tool list required for models to answer the question, we refer to it as "No Updates to Answer" -- as shown in Figure 10, all models except for Granite-4.0-h-Small-32B experience a clear drop in performance under policy constraints that restrict access to the most relevant information source (i.e. "Policy updates the answer").

In general, we find that models either violate constraints or fail to retrieve sufficient information, where they sometimes understood the policy but could not answer the question correctly, or they exhibit one of the previously analyzed failure modes.

Overall, tool-use policy-constrained settings suggest that while models can reason over tools and sources, they struggle to incorporate external constraints into that reasoning - often a key requirement for reliable real-world deployment.

VAKRA exposes a critical gap between surface-level tool competence and robust, end‑to‑end agent reliability. Although modern models can increasingly select APIs and execute isolated tool calls, VAKRA shows that these abilities alone are insufficient for real‑world deployment. In practice, models often break down when required to perform compositional reasoning under execution constraints—spanning APIs, documents, dialog context, and policy requirements.

Think your agent is solid? Put it to the test.

Run it on VAKRA and see where it falls apart—tool selection, multi-hop reasoning, or policy constraints.

👉 Try it and tell us what your agent learned

#10345. Native Model Authoring for Edge with LiteRT Tensor API

Shipping on-device AI means meeting tight latency and memory budgets on every device you target. The most common path for deploying models in production is converting a trained model, for example converting a PyTorch model with LiteRT Torch, and running it with the LiteRT runtime. This offers the quickest and most reliable route to production, and it's the path we recommend for most projects. Sometimes, though, developers want full control over how a network is represented and optimized to support new architectures or to try a new lowering logic without waiting for upstream framework updates.

For ultimate control, developers write computations manually in native C++ or shader languages. Apple's MLX made this code-first approach popular on Apple silicon, and llama.cpp showed how far tailored C++ implementations can take LLM inference. However, the level of control comes at a significant cost: implementations are tightly coupled to specific backends (such as Metal, OpenCL, or Vulkan) and must be rewritten for each new hardware target. Furthermore, managing zero-copy buffer interoperability and synchronization across CPU, GPU, and NPU, while gluing together pre-processing, inference, and post-processing, demands substantial manual engineering effort.

To solve the above challenges, we are excited to announce the release of the novel LiteRT Tensor API, a lightweight authoring layer in the LiteRT stack, designed to improve handcrafting models. It combines the flexibility of native authoring with cross-platform portability. You build the computation graph op by op in C++, choosing exactly which ops run and how they connect. The same graph can run through LiteRT on CPU, GPU (powered by open-source ML Drift) and NPU, or without model file or runtime directly on CPU through XNNPACK, so you don't rewrite it for each new hardware target. Model inference and pre/post-processing can be assembled with the same API and chained through shared accelerator buffers, so that data never round-trips through the CPU. Start with the conversion path, which remains the best default for most models. Reach for the Tensor API when you need low-level control over the graph or want the whole pipeline to run end to end on the accelerator.

The LiteRT Tensor API also serves as an ideal programmatic foundation for AI coding agents, providing structured primitives to generate, rewire, and tune model graphs automatically. In the rest of this post, we’ll dive into the design and walk through practical code examples showing how to author models from scratch.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

To show the Tensor API in practice, we built an interactive Segment Anything App, running entirely on-device in the browser on WebGPU. The app enables real-time multi-object segmentation and tracking via Meta's Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2), triggered either by simple clicks or natural language prompts powered by Gemma 4 E2B.

The SAM 2 model is fully authored in C++ via the LiteRT Tensor API. A coding agent wrote and evolved it from under 10 to over 30 frames per second at 512x512 on WebGPU. See that the complete implementation and the web app are open source in the LiteRT Samples GitHub repo.

The LiteRT Tensor API provides four key features for authoring and optimizing on-device models:

We ran the same C++ code for the SAM 2 model on the GPUs of three devices: a macOS laptop (Metal), an iOS phone (Metal), and an Android phone (OpenCL). In our tests on the MacBook Pro, it ran about 1.5x faster than Apple MLX (fp16, image encoder plus mask decoder). The SAM 2.1 sample includes the benchmark commands so you can reproduce the results.

With the Tensor API, each layer is a C++ function over Tensor values, built from high-level operators and weights loaded directly from the checkpoint. For example, here is a multi-head self-attention layer:

In the SAM 2 sample, BuildEncoder and BuildDecoder compose layers like this into the encoder and decoder graphs, and ModelFactory exports both as two signatures of one sam2_image.tflite file.

A .tflite file is one of two ways to run your graph. The backend is a template argument on Tensor: TfLiteMixinTag exports a .tflite that LiteRT runs on CPU, ML Drift (GPU), or NPU, and XnnpackMixinTag runs the same code directly on CPU through XNNPACK, with no model file. Tag tensors with both to keep both options:

SAM 2 takes the .tflite path to reach WebGPU in the browser, and the rest of this post follows it. The Gemma 4 example takes the direct path for prefill and decode on CPU, the lightest way to run Tensor API code. The Tensor API README walks through both.

A natural workflow uses both: iterate on the direct XNNPACK path, loading weights straight from the .safetensors checkpoint with no model file to rebuild, then export a .tflite when you're ready to ship with LiteRT on mobile or on the web through LiteRT.js.

A real app needs more than the neural network itself. In the demo, turning a camera frame and a click into a mask takes four steps: pre-processing converts the frame into the 512x512 image the model expects; the image encoder turns that image into features; the mask decoder combines those features with the click to predict a mask; and post-processing scales the mask back to the frame's size. Running this whole pipeline fast takes two things: keeping data on the accelerator (such as the GPU) between steps, and controlling how each step runs on each accelerator.

In a typical app, only the model runs on the GPU; the CPU resizes each camera frame, passes the encoder's output to the decoder, and post-processes the mask. Each trip copies data and stalls the GPU.

In litert-samples/sam2, all four steps are Tensor API graphs on the GPU. Pre-processing, for example, is a small graph built with CreateLambdaRunner. The graphs are connected once at startup to share buffers, then run for each frame and click:

No data returns to the CPU between steps: all 522 encoder and 269 decoder operations run on the GPU, and pre- and post-processing add only about 0.34 ms per frame.

Because the graph is plain C++, you or your coding agent can rewrite it for each backend. Our agent, Antigravity, moved SAM 2's per-frame decisions, such as whether the object is still visible, from CPU code into the graph. Comparisons like score > 0 would still fall back to the CPU on WebGPU, because they output true/false values, so the agent rewrote them as arithmetic in StepPos:

Each object now takes a single GPU call per frame. The agent made a series of changes like this, such as folding the attention scale into the weights, and checked each against Hugging Face's SAM 2 before keeping it. That's how we more than tripled the model's frame rate.

We're working on direct ML Drift (GPU) backends, NPU-friendly operations, and automatic full-graph quantization. We're also adding Python authoring with .tflite export, plus wider dynamic-shape support for varying image sizes, batch sizes, and sequence lengths.

Explore our resources and start your journey with LiteRT:

The LiteRT Tensor API and its reference implementations are the result of a collaborative effort across the Google AI Edge and LiteRT teams. Special thanks to Byungchul Kim, Changming Sun, Chenchen Tang, Dillon Sharlet, Jingjiang Li, Lu Wang, Lutz Justen, Matthias Grundmann, Misha Gutman, Ronald Wotzlaw, and Sachin Kotwani.

#10343. Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. In my previous blogpost, I introduced the new multimodal capabilities, showing how to use embedding and reranker models that handle text, images, audio, and video. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to train or finetune these multimodal models on your own data.

As a practical example, I'll walk through finetuning Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for Visual Document Retrieval (VDR), the task of retrieving relevant document pages (as images, with charts, tables, and layout intact) for a given text query. The resulting tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr demonstrates how much performance you can gain by finetuning on your own domain. On my evaluation data, the finetuned model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 compared to the base model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models I tested against, including models up to 4x its size.

If you're new to multimodal models in Sentence Transformers, I recommend reading Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers first. For training text-only embedding, reranker, or sparse embedding models, see the Prior Blogposts section at the end.

General-purpose multimodal embedding models like Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B are trained on diverse data to perform well across a wide range of languages and tasks: image-text matching, visual question answering, document understanding, and more. But this generality means the model is rarely the best choice for any specific task.

Consider Visual Document Retrieval: given a text query like "What was the company's Q3 revenue?", the model must find the most relevant document screenshot from a corpus of thousands. This requires understanding document layouts, charts, tables, and text, which is a very different skill from e.g. matching pictures of shoes with product descriptions.

By finetuning on domain-specific data, the model can learn these specialized patterns. In my experiment, finetuning improved NDCG@10 from 0.888 to 0.947, ahead of every recent multimodal model I tested, including ones up to 4x larger.

Training multimodal Sentence Transformer models involves the same components as training text-only models:

The multimodal training pipeline uses the same SentenceTransformerTrainer as text-only training. The key difference is that your datasets contain images (or other modalities) alongside text, and the model's processor handles the image preprocessing automatically.

Let's walk through each component, using Visual Document Retrieval (matching text queries to document screenshots) as a running example.

The most common approach is to finetune an existing multimodal embedding model, or to start from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) checkpoint. The Transformer module automatically detects supported modalities from the model's processor.

To finetune an existing multimodal embedding model (e.g. one that already has a modules.json file), you can pass processor_kwargs and model_kwargs to control preprocessing and model loading respectively. processor_kwargs are passed directly to AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(...) (e.g., image resolution bounds: higher max_pixels means higher quality but more memory), while model_kwargs are passed to the appropriate AutoModel.from_pretrained(...) call (e.g., precision, attention implementation):

You can also start from a fresh VLM checkpoint that hasn't been trained for embeddings yet. Sentence Transformers will attempt to recognize the architecture, infer the supported modalities from the processor, and set up the appropriate forward method and pooling. If the automatic detection doesn't work perfectly for a particular model, the configuration in the saved sentence_bert_config.json can be edited to adjust modality settings, forward methods, and output handling:

In both cases, the Transformer module inspects the processor to determine which modalities are available, and Pooling is added automatically if needed. You can verify the supported modalities:

Instead of using a single VLM backbone, you can compose separate encoders for different modalities using the Router module. This lets you combine any existing encoders and route inputs to the appropriate one based on detected modality:

Since Router-based multimodal models use separate encoders per modality, their embedding spaces are initially unaligned. Training is required to align the spaces for meaningful cross-modal similarity. The Dense projection layer shown above helps map embeddings from different encoders into a shared space.

This approach is useful when you want to use lightweight, specialized encoders rather than a large VLM. You can also combine Router-based multimodality with task-based routing (e.g. different encoders for queries vs. documents) using route_mappings. See the Router documentation for advanced routing scenarios.

For this example, I use the tomaarsen/llamaindex-vdr-en-train-preprocessed dataset, a preprocessed English subset of llamaindex/vdr-multilingual-train. The source dataset was released alongside the Visual Document Retrieval Goes Multilingual blogpost by LlamaIndex, and consists of ~500k multilingual query-image samples collected from public internet PDFs, with queries synthetically generated using VLMs (gemini-1.5-pro and Qwen2-VL-72B). My preprocessed version filters to the 53,512 English samples and resolves 4 of the 16 ID-based hard negatives per sample into actual document screenshot images, so it can be used directly for training without further preprocessing:

The train config contains the first 10,000 samples, and the eval config contains the next 300 samples (a full config with all 53,512 samples is also available). For training, I select query, image, and negative_0 to form (anchor, positive, hard negative) triplets. Including additional hard negatives would likely improve the training signal, but each extra negative also increases memory usage and training time, so I stick with one. For evaluation, I keep all four hard negatives per query to build a more challenging retrieval corpus (more on that in the Evaluator section).

Just like text-only training, the dataset format must match your chosen loss function. The rules are the same:

For multimodal datasets, the inputs can contain:

The data collator automatically calls model.preprocess(), which detects the modality of each input and applies the appropriate preprocessing. No manual tokenization or image processing is needed.

Many Hugging Face datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers, allowing you to easily find them at https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers.

For this training, I use CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, a common choice for retrieval tasks. It accepts (query, positive) pairs with any number of additional hard negative columns, from 0 up to n, as long as each sample has the same number of negatives. During training, the loss pushes each query's similarity to its positive up and its similarity to every negative down. The negatives come from two sources:

More negatives per query means a stronger training signal, so a larger batch size directly improves training quality. Beyond that, the "cached" variant of the loss uses gradient caching to make large effective batch sizes feasible even when GPU memory is limited.

The mini_batch_size parameter controls how many samples are processed at once during the cached forward passes. For large multimodal models, setting this to a small value (e.g., 1) is important to avoid out-of-memory errors without sacrificing the benefits of large effective batch sizes:

To produce embeddings that work well at multiple dimensionalities, I wrap the base loss with MatryoshkaLoss. This trains the model so that truncating the embedding to a smaller number of dimensions still yields good performance:

This is especially useful for multimodal models, where embeddings can be large (2048 dimensions for Qwen3-VL). With Matryoshka training, you can use truncated embeddings (e.g., 256 or 128 dimensions) at deployment time for faster search with minimal quality loss. As I'll show in the Results section, the finetuned model achieves near-peak performance even at 512 dimensions.

The SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments class lets you control training hyperparameters. Here's the configuration used for the VDR finetuning:

A few things to note for (multimodal) training:

To track retrieval performance before, during, and after training, I use the InformationRetrievalEvaluator. It computes standard retrieval metrics like NDCG@10, MAP, and Recall@k:

The evaluator takes text queries, a corpus of images (including hard negatives), and a mapping of which documents are relevant to which queries. Note that the corpus contains a mix of positive and hard negative document screenshots, making this a challenging evaluation. Using batch_size=1 prevents out-of-memory issues during evaluation of the large VLM.

The SentenceTransformerTrainer brings everything together. Here's the complete training script:

The training script is nearly identical to a text-only training script. The only differences are:

Everything else (the trainer, training arguments, dataset loading) works exactly the same as text-only training.

After training for just 1 epoch, the finetuned tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 on the evaluation set (300 queries, 1500 corpus documents, cosine similarity). This is a significant improvement over the base Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models:

The finetuned 2B model outperforms even the 8B Qwen3-VL-Embedding model, demonstrating the power of task-specific finetuning. Finetuning on your own domain is often worth considering, even when a larger general-purpose model is available!

The comparison above uses full-size 2048-dim embeddings. Thanks to the Matryoshka training, the finetuned model also holds up well when truncated to fewer dimensions, letting you trade off embedding size and retrieval quality at deployment time:

The finetuned model's peak is at the full 2048 dimensions (0.948), but it stays within 0.3% of peak all the way down to 512 (4x smaller), and retains over 92% of peak even at 64 (32x smaller). Matryoshka training concentrates the most important information in the earlier dimensions, so moderate truncation costs very little performance.

The gap between 1024 and 2048 dimensions is small (0.946 vs. 0.948), so I've saved the model with truncate_dim=1024 set in its configuration. This means that SentenceTransformer("tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr") produces 1024-dimensional embeddings by default, halving the storage footprint compared to the full 2048. If you want a different dimensionality, pass truncate_dim=N when loading to override it.

You can also finetune multimodal Cross Encoder (reranker) models using the same training infrastructure. The key difference is using CrossEncoderTrainer and Cross Encoder-specific loss functions. This section provides a brief overview; see the full training examples for complete, runnable scripts with dataset preparation and evaluation.

Here's a simplified example based on the doodles training script, which trains a reranker to match images with text captions:

There are multiple valid architectural choices for multimodal rerankers, including:

Both approaches are demonstrated in the multimodal cross encoder training examples.

The two scripts linked above split the training data into two datasets, one per direction (image-to-text and text-to-image), with a task-specific prompt for each that tells the model how to score in that direction. Each positive pair is then expanded with randomly sampled negatives so the loss sees a balanced mix of matches and non-matches.

The Sentence Transformers repository includes several multimodal training examples:

Additionally, the following pages may be useful to learn more about training with Sentence Transformers:

The direct prerequisite and the prior training guides are listed first, followed by related technique posts that stack with multimodal training:

#10342. AI-Powered Pentesting for DevSecOps: 7 Checks Developers Should Make First

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Security testing used to happen once or twice a year, usually after a release had already shipped. That rhythm does not fit teams that deploy daily. AI-assisted tools now promise testing that runs continuously, chains steps together on its own, and writes up what it found.

For developers, the interesting question is not whether these tools are impressive. It is what has to be true in your pipeline before you let an automated attacker loose on your own systems. This article covers seven checks to make first, each with a pass condition, and one short code example you can run. Some checks, such as written authorization and cost tracking, usually belong to a security lead or manager. For those, the developer's job is to confirm they exist, not to own them.

Testing systems you do not have permission to test is not a gray area. Make sure someone with authority has approved the targets and the time window, and keep that approval with your records. Run the first tests against staging with test data. Production comes later, once you know how the tool behaves and what load it creates.

Pass: The approval is on file, and the SOC knows the window and source IPs.

An automated tester should never decide for itself what it is allowed to touch. Define scope in a file that your pipeline can check: which hosts are in bounds, when testing may run, and whether anything destructive is allowed.

SitePoint's article on security patterns for autonomous agents uses an open-source AI penetration-testing agent as its case study. It covers sandboxed execution, tool permissions scoped to each role, approval gates for high-risk actions, and audit logging. Scope enforcement belongs in that same family of controls. Here is a minimal check that refuses any target outside the allowlist or time window:

Call this before every scan job, and log the result. A tool that is out of bounds should fail loudly instead of quietly continuing.

Pass: An out-of-scope target fails the job, and egress outside the allowlist is blocked.

Findings are only useful if they reach the people who can fix them. Most teams already have a place where security results show up in pull requests or a security tab. SitePoint's walkthrough on automating DevSecOps static analysis with GitHub Actions shows how results written in the SARIF format appear as inline annotations and can block a merge when severity crosses a threshold. If your pentest tool can export SARIF or a similar format, send its findings to the same place.

Pass: The tool exports SARIF or similar, and results show up in PRs or the security tab.

An AI tool can produce a long list of findings. To judge whether they are complete and sensible, you need a reference for what good web security testing covers. The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide is a free, widely used checklist of test categories for web applications. It covers web applications only, so APIs and network services exposed to the internet need their own coverage. Map the tool's findings against it, and note which categories it never touched.

Pass: You know which OWASP WSTG categories you expect the tool to cover.

Vendors describe AI pentesting in similar terms: agents plan attack steps, try them, and verify what works. For a view of how a security vendor explains the approach, CyCognito's overview of AI penetration testing walks through a workflow from scoping to autonomous testing, validation and reporting, and notes that human review stays part of the process. All vendor claims need testing in a demo against your own systems before you rely on them.

Ask the same questions of any tool you evaluate: What does it test beyond known checks? How does it confirm a finding is real? What does it send to external services?

Pass: The vendor has clear answers, including where the target list comes from.

Automated findings need review. A person should confirm that a reported path is exploitable, judge its business impact, and decide the fix order. Make sure this is set up before the first run. Without it, a team can end up with a long backlog of unverified findings and little trust in the tool.

Pass: There is a named reviewer and time set aside each cycle.

Running agents continuously can add up, especially when they call large models. Make sure you can track what each run costs and how many real issues it finds, so you can compare it with other approaches. You also need to be able to rerun the specific test that found a problem after a fix ships and keep the result. A finding is only closed when the retest passes.

Pass: Both are possible before you commit to running the tool continuously.

Does AI pentesting replace manual penetration testing?

Not entirely. Automated testing can run more often and cover more ground, but people are still needed for scoping, complex attack paths and judging impact.

In staging, with test data, inside a written scope and time window.

What should I do with findings from the tool?

Send them to the same place as your other security results, have the named reviewer check them, and retest after fixes.

AI-assisted pentesting can give development teams faster and more frequent security feedback, but only when it runs inside clear limits. Before the first run, check that targets and the window are approved, scope is enforced by your pipeline, findings will land where developers work, you have a baseline to judge the output, you know what the tool tests and sends out, someone owns the review, and you can measure cost and retest. The scope check above is small, but it makes sure the tool stays inside the lines you set.

As high-end PC hardware continues to surge in demand and price, GPU theft has become a highly profitable target for criminals. According to a report by ABC7 News, authorities are investigating a major cargo heist involving the disappearance of an $11.4 million shipment of Nvidia hardware. The shipment reportedly consisted of six pallets of Nvidia hardware that left Oakland for Texas on August 29 and was picked up by a truck posing as a food transport company. Investigators eventually lost track of the vehicle in San Bernardino County, with the Oakland Police Department receiving a report of the theft on September 13.

"These chips command about double the price that they command inside the United States. So, if a chip costs about $550,000, then they go for about 1 million or more abroad," said Olaf Groth, a professor at UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business.

While there has been no announcement regarding any arrests, the authorities are said to be investigating the matter. The incident has also raised concerns among experts about the security of high-value technology shipments and the potential national security risks posed by advanced computing hardware making its way into black-market channels.

In a similar incident from Brazil back in September, two pallets containing Nvidia's top-of-the-line GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards, valued at approximately $470,000 (R$2.5 million), disappeared at Guarulhos International Airport in São Paulo. The shipment, imported from the US, had reportedly arrived at the airport on September 20 and cleared customs on September 24, but the two pallets went missing the following day after being authorized for release.

The investigation eventually uncovered a possible inside job, with Brazilian police identifying three airport employees suspected of helping carry out the heist. According to reports, two outsourced forklift operators allegedly removed the pallets from a warehouse, an incident that was reportedly captured on CCTV, while a third employee responsible for checking and releasing merchandise allegedly helped bypass the airport's electronic controls.

Things took an interesting turn when one of the stolen Zotac RTX 5090 graphics cards appeared for sale on the Brazilian online marketplace OLX for more than $6,000. The listing included clear pictures of the card's serial number, allowing it to be linked to the missing shipment. The listing has since been taken down, while the whereabouts of the remaining graphics cards remain unclear.

#10340. Two more Garmin smartwatches are down to record-low prices

The Garmin Fenix E and Garmin Venu 3S are for two different types of people, but both are available at a surprisingly low price thanks to these limited-time Garmin deals.

Garmin watches are often expensive, which is why I always recommend them on sale. For example, the Garmin Fenix E, usually $799, is now down to $399. That’s the all-time low price for this model and probably the best Garmin deal I’ve seen so far this fall.

The Garmin Fenix E is essentially a Garmin Epix Gen 2 with a newer OS. It sports multi-GNSS navigation plus a 3-axis compass, gyroscope, and barometric altimeter that should cover basically all your tracking needs. It’s got pulse ox monitoring, respiration tracking, advanced sleep monitoring, real-time stamina tracking, and a training readiness score (so you know what days you should be taking it easy).

Despite all the features, this one will last you two weeks per charge and can utilize GPS for up to 42 hours on each charge. The stainless steel bezel looks great, and the 47mm fiber-reinforced polymer case is built to last. This is one of those watches that, quite frankly, makes no sense at full cost. At half the price, though? Yeah, that looks much better.

If you’re looking for something a little more elegant-looking, the Garmin Venu 3S is the right choice. At $299, this Garmin deal makes it $250 less than the Garmin Venu 4. You might think buying the newest one is automatically better, but that’s not necessarily the case between these two models.

For example, the Venu 4 is thicker and heavier because it uses an all-metal casing, has one less button on the side, lacks the permanent hour markers that are on the Venu 3S’s bezel, and has worse battery life by 1-2 days, depending on your usage. The Venu 4 has more features and a newer OS, but I personally like the OS design on the 3S better (and I’m apparently not alone on that front).

The Venu 4 also has new sleep guidance and coaching features, training load and several tools that used to be for Garmin Forerunner watches, plus lifestyle logging, but I’m not sure I’d want to pay $250 to get those. Either way, you’ve got a great option now that the Venu 3S is at such a fantastic price.
